\section{Propositions as Types}
\label{sec:curry-howard}

A theorem prover has to decide whether a proof is correct. A proof written in English cannot be checked by a computer, 
and the Curry--Howard correspondence is exactly the concept that connects logic with programming:
\emph{propositions are types, and proofs are programs}.
A proposition $A$ is true if we can construct a term $t$ of type $A$, written $t : A$.

For example, consider the proposition $A \to B$ (``$A$ implies $B$'').
To prove it, we assume $A$ and construct a proof of $B$.
This is exactly a function that takes a value of type $A$ and returns a value of type $B$.
Thus, logical implication corresponds to a function type. Here are three examples, where $\lambda x.\,e$ denotes a 
function taking $x$ and returning $e$:

\[
\begin{array}{rcll}
P \to P
&:& \lambda p.\,p
& \text{Return the assumption.}\\[4pt]
A \to B \to A
&:& \lambda a.\,\lambda b.\,a
& \text{Ignore the second argument.}\\[4pt]
(A \to B) \to (B \to C) \to A \to C
&:& \lambda f.\,\lambda g.\,\lambda a.\,g(f(a))
& \text{Compose two functions.}
\end{array}
\]

The same idea extends to universal quantification.
To prove ``for every $x : A$, $B(x)$ holds'', we construct a function
that takes any $x : A$ and returns a proof of $B(x)$. Unlike an ordinary function type $A \to B$, the return type $B(x)$
may depend on the input $x$. This is called a \emph{dependent function type},
written
\[
\Pi(x : A).\,B(x).
\]
For example, ``every proposition implies itself'' is expressed as
\[
\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P},
\]
where $\Sort{0}$ is the type of propositions. Its proof is simply
\[
\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}.
\]

This gives us the central idea behind a theorem prover:
\emph{proving a theorem means constructing a term of the required type,
and verifying a proof means type-checking that term}.
The kernel implements these typing rules rather than reasoning about
truth directly.

\section{Syntax}
\label{sec:syntax}

We begin with a small dependent type theory consisting of five kinds of terms:
\[
t, A, B ::= \Sort{u} \mid x \mid \tPi{x}{A}{B} \mid \tLam{x}{A}{t} \mid t\;s
\]
Here, $u$ is a natural number and $x$ is a variable name.
Throughout, $s, t, a, b, f, A, B, C, T$ (possibly with subscripts or primes) stand for terms,
$x, y, z$ and the other names bound by $\Pi$ or $\lambda$ stand for variable names, and $u, v$ stand for universe levels.
Accordingly, the set $\FV(t)$ of free variables of a term $t$, defined in \S\ref{sec:subst}, is a set of names.

\begin{itemize}
    \item $\Sort{u}$: A universe containing types.
    \item $x$: A variable.
    \item $\tPi{x}{A}{B}$: A \emph{$\Pi$-type} (dependent function type), whose result type $B$ may depend on $x$.
    \item $\tLam{x}{A}{t}$: A \emph{$\lambda$-abstraction}, i.e.\ a function that takes $x : A$ and returns $t$.
    \item $t\;s$: Function application.
\end{itemize}

\noindent When $B$ does not depend on $x$, we write $A \to B$ instead of
$\tPi{x}{A}{B}$. Thus, ordinary function types are special cases
of dependent function types. For example, the proposition ``every proposition implies itself''
and its proof are represented as
\[
\underbrace{\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}}_{\text{proof}}
\quad : \quad
\underbrace{\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}_{\text{proposition = type of proof}}.
\]
Notice that types and expressions share the same grammar.
There is no separate syntax for types: whether a term is a valid
type is determined by the type checker.

Application associates to the left and arrows associate to the right: $f\;a\;b$ means $(f\;a)\;b$, and
$A \to B \to C$ means $A \to (B \to C)$. A function of two arguments is thus a function that takes the first
argument and returns a function expecting the second; this encoding is called \emph{currying}. For example,
$\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}}$ has type $A \to B \to A$, and applied to $x : A$ and $y : B$ it is written
$(\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}})\;x\;y$, that is, $((\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}})\;x)\;y$.


\section{Typing Rules}
\label{sec:typing}

\paragraph{Contexts and judgments.}
A \emph{context} $\Gamma$ is an ordered list of assumptions $x_1 : A_1, \ldots, x_n : A_n$.
It records the type of each variable in scope, and we write $\dom(\Gamma)$ for the set $\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$.
Since \textsc{C-Ext} below forbids repeated names, $\Gamma$ can be used like a dictionary from names to types,
and \textsc{T-Var} is simply a lookup.
Unlike a plain dictionary, however, the order matters: $A_i$ may mention $x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}$, as in $P : \Sort{0}, h : P$.
We use two judgments:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\ctxok{\Gamma}$: the context $\Gamma$ is well formed.
  \item $\Gamma \vdash t : A$: under the assumptions in $\Gamma$, the term $t$ has type $A$.
\end{itemize}
Read through Curry--Howard, $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ says that $t$ is a proof of $A$ from the hypotheses $\Gamma$.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\begin{mathpar}
\inferrule{\quad}{\ctxok{\cdot}}\rulename{C-Empty}
\and
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma} \\ \Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ x \notin \dom(\Gamma)}{\ctxok{\Gamma, x : A}}\rulename{C-Ext}
\\
\and
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}}\rulename{T-Sort}
\and
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma} \\ (x : A) \in \Gamma}{\Gamma \vdash x : A}\rulename{T-Var}
\\
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \Sort{v}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \Sort{\imax(u, v)}}\rulename{T-Pi}
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash t : B}{\Gamma \vdash \tLam{x}{A}{t} : \tPi{x}{A}{B}}\rulename{T-Lam}
\\
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{A}{B} \\ \Gamma \vdash a : A}{\Gamma \vdash f\;a : \subst{B}{x}{a}}\rulename{T-App}
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash t : A \\ \Gamma \vdash B : \Sort{u} \\ A \conv B}{\Gamma \vdash t : B}\rulename{T-Conv}
\end{mathpar}
\caption{Well-formed contexts and typing rules.}
\label{fig:typing}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Two operations used by the rules.}
Two of the rules rely on operations on terms that we treat as black boxes for now.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Substitution.} \textsc{T-App} writes $\subst{B}{x}{a}$ for $B$ with every free occurrence of $x$ replaced by $a$.
    For example, $\subst{(P \to P)}{P}{Q} = Q \to Q$.
    Replacing names inside binders needs some care, which \S\ref{sec:subst} explains.
  \item \emph{Definitional equality.} \textsc{T-Conv} writes $A \conv B$ when $A$ and $B$ are ``the same type'' in a sense the kernel can decide.
    Two kinds of differences are ignored.
    First, the names of bound variables: $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$ and $\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{Q \to Q}$ state the same proposition.
    Terms that differ only in this way are called \emph{$\alpha$-equivalent}, written $\alphaeq$.
    Second, computation: if $\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$, then $\mathit{Id}\;P$ computes to $P$ by plugging $P$ in for $X$,
    so a proof of $\mathit{Id}\;P$ should also count as a proof of $P$.
    This computation step, $(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s \betared \subst{t}{x}{s}$, is called \emph{$\beta$-reduction}.
\end{itemize}
The kernel decides $A \conv B$ by computing both sides as far as possible ($\beta$-reducing) and then checking whether the results are $\alpha$-equivalent.
\S\ref{sec:machinery} defines both operations precisely and gives the algorithms; until then, an intuitive reading is enough.

We read each rule from the bottom up, as a recipe for checking a term.

\begin{description}
  \item[\textsc{C-Empty}, \textsc{C-Ext}.]
    A context is built one assumption at a time, and each new assumption must have a type as its type.
    The side condition $x \notin \dom(\Gamma)$ forbids shadowing inside a context.
    Since the names of bound variables do not matter, this is no restriction on terms: a binder that would shadow can always be renamed first.
    \S\ref{sec:capture} shows why this condition matters.
  \item[\textsc{T-Sort}.]
    Every universe lives in the next one; see \S\ref{sec:universes} for why.
  \item[\textsc{T-Var}.]
    A variable has the type it was assumed to have. Logically, this is ``use a hypothesis''.
  \item[\textsc{T-Pi}.]
    $\tPi{x}{A}{B}$ is a type if $A$ is a type and $B$ is a type once we assume $x : A$.
    It lives in the larger of the two universes, except that it is a proposition whenever $B$ is one;
    $\imax(u, v)$ is $0$ if $v = 0$ and $\max(u, v)$ otherwise (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).
    Logically, this rule says when $A \to B$ and $\forall x{:}A.\,B$ are well-formed propositions.
  \item[\textsc{T-Lam}.]
    To build a function from $A$ to $B$, assume $x : A$ and build $t : B$.
    Logically, this is the introduction rule for $\to$ and $\forall$: to prove $A \to B$, assume $A$ and prove $B$.
    Note that $B$ may mention $x$, and it is kept as is in the resulting $\Pi$ type.
  \item[\textsc{T-App}.]
    If $f$ maps each $x : A$ to an element of $B$, and $a : A$, then $f\;a$ has type $B$ with $x$ replaced by $a$.
    Logically, this is modus ponens when $B$ does not mention $x$, and instantiation of a universal statement when it does.
    For example, if $f : \tPi{n}{\mathsf{Nat}}{n + 0 = n}$, then $f\;3 : 3 + 0 = 3$ (natural numbers are added in \S\ref{sec:inductive}).
  \item[\textsc{T-Conv}.]
    Types that are equal up to computation are interchangeable.
    For example, from $h : \mathit{Id}\;P$ we may conclude $h : P$.
    This is the only rule that is not determined by the shape of $t$.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Why application matters.}
Without \textsc{T-App}, a hypothesis can be returned but never used.
Roughly, the provable propositions are then those whose conclusion is literally one of the hypotheses, such as $P \to Q \to P$.
Composition, $(P \to Q) \to (Q \to R) \to P \to R$, has the proof
$\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{g}{Q \to R}{\tLam{p}{P}{g\,(f\,p)}}}$, which needs application.

\section{The Typing Rules as a Logic}
\label{sec:logic}

The typing rules of \S\ref{sec:typing} are meant to be rules of logic.
This section makes that claim precise, and identifies the property, consistency, that a trustworthy kernel must have.

Consider the logic whose formulas are built from proposition variables $P, Q, \ldots$ by implication and quantification over propositions:
\[
\varphi, \psi ::= P \mid \varphi \to \psi \mid \forall P.\,\varphi
\]
This is second-order propositional logic.
Its proofs are natural-deduction derivations of judgments $\Delta \vdash \varphi$, where $\Delta$ is a list of hypotheses.
Each formula translates to a type, and each list of hypotheses to a context:
\[
P^\ast = P, \qquad
(\varphi \to \psi)^\ast = \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast, \qquad
(\forall P.\,\varphi)^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast},
\]
\[
(\varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_n)^\ast = P_1 : \Sort{0}, \ldots, P_k : \Sort{0},\; h_1 : \varphi_1^\ast, \ldots, h_n : \varphi_n^\ast,
\]
where $P_1, \ldots, P_k$ are the proposition variables free in $\Delta$ or in the conclusion $\varphi$ of the judgment $\Delta \vdash \varphi$ being translated,
and $h_1, \ldots, h_n$ are fresh names for the hypotheses.
The conclusion must be included because a proposition variable may occur only there, as $P$ does in $\cdot \vdash P \to P$.
Fig.~\ref{fig:logic} places each logical rule next to the typing rule it corresponds to; in each row, $\Delta^\ast$ is the context for the conclusion of the rule.
Erasing the terms from the right column gives the left column exactly.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{3.2}
\begin{tabular}{@{}r@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c@{}}
& \textbf{Logic} & \textbf{Type theory} \\
Hypothesis &
$\inferrule{\varphi_i \in \Delta}{\Delta \vdash \varphi_i}$ &
$\inferrule{(h_i : \varphi_i^\ast) \in \Delta^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash h_i : \varphi_i^\ast}\rulename{T-Var}$ \\
$\to$-intro &
$\inferrule{\Delta, \varphi \vdash \psi}{\Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast, h : \varphi^\ast \vdash t : \psi^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash \tLam{h}{\varphi^\ast}{t} : \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast}\rulename{T-Lam}$ \\
$\to$-elim &
$\inferrule{\Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi \\ \Delta \vdash \varphi}{\Delta \vdash \psi}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast \vdash f : \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast \\ \Delta^\ast \vdash a : \varphi^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash f\;a : \psi^\ast}\rulename{T-App}$ \\
$\forall$-intro &
$\inferrule{\Delta \vdash \varphi \\ P \notin \FV(\Delta)}{\Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast, P : \Sort{0} \vdash t : \varphi^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{t} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}}\rulename{T-Lam}$ \\
$\forall$-elim &
$\inferrule{\Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}{\Delta \vdash \subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi}}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast \vdash f : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast} \\ \Delta^\ast \vdash \psi^\ast : \Sort{0}}{\Delta^\ast \vdash f\;\psi^\ast : \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast}}\rulename{T-App}$
\end{tabular}
\caption{Natural deduction (left) and the typing rules that implement it (right). Premises that only check that a type is well formed are omitted.}
\label{fig:logic}
\end{figure}

In the $\forall$-intro row, the side condition $P \notin \FV(\Delta)$ guarantees that no hypothesis mentions $P$,
so the typing rule may add $P : \Sort{0}$ after the hypotheses.
In the $\forall$-elim row, the premise $\psi^\ast : \Sort{0}$ holds for every formula $\psi$, even one that contains $\forall$,
because \textsc{T-Pi} places every translated formula in $\Sort{0}$ (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).
Hence $\forall$-elim may instantiate $P$ with any formula, as in the logic.

\begin{theorem}[Proofs are terms]
\label{thm:pat}
If $\Delta \vdash \varphi$ is provable, then $\Delta^\ast \vdash t : \varphi^\ast$ for some term $t$.
\end{theorem}

\noindent The figure turns each step of a proof into a step of a typing derivation, so every proof becomes a term.
Appendix~\ref{app:pat} states the theorem precisely and gives the full proof.

The theorem says that the type checker can check every proof of the logic.
For the type checker to be trustworthy, we also need the opposite guarantee: it must not accept a term for a proposition that the logic refutes.
Define $\bot = \forall P.\,P$ (``everything holds'').
No proof of $\bot$ exists: if each $P$ is read as true or false, every rule preserves truth under every reading, but $\forall P.\,P$ is false.
The type theory should agree, that is, no closed term should have type
\[
\bot^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}.
\]
A closed term $t : \bot^\ast$ would prove every proposition, since $t\;C : C$ for every $C : \Sort{0}$.
A system in which no closed term has type $\bot^\ast$ is called \emph{consistent}, and a design for universes is acceptable only if the system remains consistent (\S\ref{sec:universes}).
\S\ref{sec:properties} states consistency for our system as Theorem~\ref{thm:consistency}.

One might hope for the full converse of Theorem~\ref{thm:pat}: every term of type $\varphi^\ast$ comes from a proof of $\varphi$.
That is a stronger property, called conservativity, and it is harder to establish here,
because $\Sort{0}$ also contains types that are not translations of formulas, such as $\tPi{F}{\Sort{0} \to \Sort{0}}{F\;P \to F\;P}$, and a term may pass through them.
We do not need it; consistency is enough.

\section{A Type Checking Algorithm}
\label{sec:algorithm}

The rules in Fig.~\ref{fig:typing} define which judgments hold, but they are not yet an algorithm.
The first five typing rules are triggered by the shape of the term: a $\Sort{}$, a variable, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or an application.
\textsc{T-Conv} has no such trigger; it may be applied at any point, so a program cannot tell when to use it.
The standard solution splits type checking into two mutually recursive functions~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}:
\textsc{Infer} computes the type of a term, and \textsc{Check} verifies a term against an expected type.
Definitional equality is used only where two types must be compared: in \textsc{Check}, and when a type must have a particular shape (a $\Pi$ or a $\mathsf{Sort}$).

The algorithm calls two functions on terms, whose definitions we postpone to \S\ref{sec:machinery}:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\textsc{Whnf}(T)$ computes $T$ until its outermost shape is visible. For example, $\textsc{Whnf}(\mathit{Id}\;(P \to P)) = P \to P$, which is a $\Pi$.
  \item $\textsc{IsDefEq}(A, B)$ decides $A \conv B$.
\end{itemize}

\begin{algorithm}[ht]
\footnotesize
\caption{Type inference and checking. \textsc{Whnf} and \textsc{IsDefEq} are defined in Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf}.}
\label{alg:infer}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Function{Infer}{$\Gamma, t$}
  \If{$t = \Sort{u}$} \Return $\Sort{(u+1)}$ \Comment{\textsc{T-Sort}}
  \ElsIf{$t = x$} \Comment{\textsc{T-Var}}
    \If{$(x : A) \in \Gamma$} \Return $A$ \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``unbound variable'' \EndIf
  \ElsIf{$t = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$} \Comment{\textsc{T-Pi}}
    \State $u \gets \Call{InferSort}{\Gamma, A}$
    \State $(x', B') \gets \Call{Freshen}{\Gamma, x, B}$
    \State $v \gets \Call{InferSort}{(\Gamma, x' : A), B'}$
    \State \Return $\Sort{\imax(u, v)}$
  \ElsIf{$t = \tLam{x}{A}{s}$} \Comment{\textsc{T-Lam}}
    \State $\Call{InferSort}{\Gamma, A}$
    \State $(x', s') \gets \Call{Freshen}{\Gamma, x, s}$
    \State $B \gets \Call{Infer}{(\Gamma, x' : A), s'}$
    \State \Return $\tPi{x'}{A}{B}$
  \ElsIf{$t = f\;a$} \Comment{\textsc{T-App}}
    \State $T \gets \textsc{Whnf}(\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma, f))$
    \If{$T = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$}
      \State $\Call{Check}{\Gamma, a, A}$
      \State \Return $\subst{B}{x}{a}$
    \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``not a function''
    \EndIf
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Check}{$\Gamma, t, T$} \Comment{\textsc{T-Conv}}
  \State $T' \gets \Call{Infer}{\Gamma, t}$
  \If{$\Call{IsDefEq}{T', T}$} \Return
  \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``type mismatch''
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{InferSort}{$\Gamma, A$}
  \State $T \gets \textsc{Whnf}(\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma, A))$
  \If{$T = \Sort{u}$} \Return $u$ \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``expected a type'' \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Freshen}{$\Gamma, x, b$}
  \If{$x \in \dom(\Gamma)$}
    \State choose $x' \notin \dom(\Gamma) \cup \FV(b)$
    \State \Return $(x', \subst{b}{x}{x'})$
  \Else\ \Return $(x, b)$
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} has the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Each case of \textsc{Infer} corresponds to exactly one rule of Fig.~\ref{fig:typing}, so the algorithm is \emph{syntax-directed}.
    Finding a proof may be hard, but checking a given proof is mechanical.
  \item \textsc{T-Conv} is never applied on its own. It happens inside \textsc{Check}, the only place where an inferred type meets an expected one.
  \item \textsc{InferSort} implements the premises of the form $\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}$.
    It is also how the kernel decides whether a term is a type at all: $A$ is a type exactly when its type computes to a universe.
    A $\lambda$-abstraction can never be a type, because its inferred type is always a $\Pi$.
  \item \textsc{Freshen} renames a binder whose name is already in the context, implementing the side condition of \textsc{C-Ext}.
    Here $\FV(b)$ is the set of free variables of $b$ (\S\ref{sec:subst}); \S\ref{sec:capture} shows what goes wrong without this step.
  \item Starting from the empty context, every context the algorithm builds is well formed, because each assumption is added only after \textsc{InferSort} succeeds.
    A caller that starts from a non-empty context must check that context separately.
  \item Termination depends on \textsc{Whnf} and \textsc{IsDefEq} terminating, which holds for well-typed terms by strong normalization (\S\ref{sec:properties}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Worked Examples}
\label{sec:examples}

This section runs Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} on a few small terms and relates each run to the typing rules of Fig.~\ref{fig:typing}.
To verify a proof $t$ of a theorem $T$, the kernel calls $\textsc{Check}(\cdot, t, T)$.

\paragraph{The identity proof.}
Let $\Gamma_1 = P : \Sort{0}$ and $\Gamma_2 = \Gamma_1, h : P$.
Omitting the well-formedness premises $\ctxok{\Gamma}$, the derivation of the opening example is
\[
\footnotesize
\inferrule*[right=T-Lam]
  {\inferrule*[right=T-Sort]{ }{\cdot \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{1}} \\
   \inferrule*[right=T-Lam]
     {\inferrule*[right=T-Var]{ }{\Gamma_1 \vdash P : \Sort{0}} \\
      \inferrule*[right=T-Var]{ }{\Gamma_2 \vdash h : P}}
     {\Gamma_1 \vdash \tLam{h}{P}{h} : P \to P}}
  {\cdot \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}
\]
The algorithm builds the same derivation from the bottom up.
$\textsc{Infer}(\cdot, \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}})$ makes the following calls:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=\arabic*.]
  \item $\textsc{InferSort}(\cdot, \Sort{0})$: \textsc{Infer} returns $\Sort{1}$, so the annotation is a type. \hfill (\textsc{T-Sort})
  \item $\textsc{Freshen}$ leaves $P$ unchanged, since the context is empty.
  \item $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma_1, \tLam{h}{P}{h})$, which makes three calls of its own:
  \begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=(\alph*)]
    \item $\textsc{InferSort}(\Gamma_1, P)$: \textsc{Infer} looks up $P$ and returns $\Sort{0}$. \hfill (\textsc{T-Var})
    \item $\textsc{Freshen}$ leaves $h$ unchanged.
    \item $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma_2, h)$ looks up $h$ and returns $P$. \hfill (\textsc{T-Var})
  \end{enumerate}
  It returns $\tPi{h}{P}{P}$. \hfill (inner \textsc{T-Lam})
\end{enumerate}
The outer call returns $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}$. \hfill (outer \textsc{T-Lam})

\noindent Each call that returns a type corresponds to one node of the tree, and no call uses computation.
Finally, \textsc{Check} compares the result with the stated type.
The two differ only in the name of one bound variable, because $P \to P$ abbreviates $\tPi{\_}{P}{P}$ and neither $h$ nor $\_$ occurs in the body,
so \textsc{IsDefEq} succeeds and the proof is accepted.

\paragraph{A wrong proof.}
Suppose a user claims that $t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{P}}$ proves $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$.
The kernel calls $\textsc{Check}(\cdot, t, \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P})$, which first calls \textsc{Infer}.
The calls are the same as above, except that the last one, $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma_2, P)$, returns $\Sort{0}$.
So \textsc{Infer} succeeds with
\[
\textsc{Infer}(\cdot, t) = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}}}.
\]
The term $t$ is well typed; it is just not a proof of the claimed proposition.
\textsc{Check} then compares the two types.
Neither can compute further, and no renaming of bound variables makes them equal:
the innermost body is $\Sort{0}$ on one side and $P$ on the other.
So \textsc{IsDefEq} fails and \textsc{Check} reports a type mismatch.
(\S\ref{sec:alpha} replays this comparison step by step with the algorithm that \textsc{IsDefEq} uses.)
The error is found only because the user stated the proposition to be proved.
A kernel that only ran \textsc{Infer} would accept $t$ and silently assign it a different type.

\paragraph{Using a hypothesis: modus ponens.}
The examples so far never apply a function. Consider
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\quad}l}
& t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{p}{P}{f\;p}}}} \\[2pt]
\text{against} & \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{(P \to Q) \to P \to Q}},
\end{array}
\]
which says ``if $P$ implies $Q$ and $P$ holds, then $Q$ holds''.
The four $\lambda$s extend the context to $\Gamma = P : \Sort{0}, Q : \Sort{0}, f : P \to Q, p : P$ exactly as before.
The body $f\;p$ reaches the application case of \textsc{Infer}:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=\arabic*.]
  \item $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma, f)$ returns $P \to Q$, that is, $\tPi{\_}{P}{Q}$. \textsc{Whnf} leaves it unchanged, and it is a $\Pi$.
  \item $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma, p, P)$ succeeds, since $p : P$ is in $\Gamma$.
  \item The result is $\subst{Q}{\_}{p} = Q$. The name $\_$ does not occur in $Q$, so the substitution does nothing. \hfill (\textsc{T-App})
\end{enumerate}
If the user had written $f\;f$ instead, step~2 would call $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma, f, P)$, which fails because $P \to Q$ is not $P$.

\paragraph{Instantiating a universal statement.}
In a dependent application, the substitution in \textsc{T-App} does real work.
Let $\mathit{id} = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}$ be the proof from the first example, and let $\Gamma = Q : \Sort{0}$.
Then $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma, \mathit{id}\;Q)$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=\arabic*.]
  \item infers $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}$ for $\mathit{id}$, which is already a $\Pi$;
  \item checks the argument, $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma, Q, \Sort{0})$;
  \item returns $\subst{(\tPi{h}{P}{P})}{P}{Q} = \tPi{h}{Q}{Q}$, that is, $Q \to Q$. \hfill (\textsc{T-App})
\end{enumerate}
Logically, this is $\forall$-elimination: from ``every proposition implies itself'' we obtain ``$Q$ implies $Q$''.
The type of the result depends on the \emph{value} of the argument $Q$; this is exactly what the dependent $\Pi$ type expresses.

\paragraph{Conversion.}
Recall $\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$ from \S\ref{sec:typing}.
Our system has no definitions, so $\mathit{Id}\;P$ below is shorthand for the term $(\tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X})\;P$.
Consider checking
\[
t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{h}}
\quad\text{against}\quad
\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}.
\]
\textsc{Infer} first checks that the annotation $\mathit{Id}\;P$ is a type.
$\textsc{InferSort}(\Gamma_1, \mathit{Id}\;P)$ reaches the application case of \textsc{Infer}:
the function $\tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$ has type $\tPi{X}{\Sort{0}}{\Sort{0}}$, the argument $P$ passes $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma_1, P, \Sort{0})$,
and the result is $\subst{\Sort{0}}{X}{P} = \Sort{0}$.
The body $h$ then has type $\mathit{Id}\;P$, so
\[
\textsc{Infer}(\cdot, t) = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{\mathit{Id}\;P}}.
\]
Renaming bound variables alone does not turn this into $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$.
But \textsc{IsDefEq} computes both sides before comparing them, and $\mathit{Id}\;P \betared P$,
so the inferred type becomes $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}$ and the comparison succeeds as in the first example.
In the typing rules, this step is an application of \textsc{T-Conv} at the root of the derivation:
\[
\footnotesize
\inferrule*[right=T-Conv]
  {\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\mathit{Id}\;P \to \mathit{Id}\;P} \\
   \cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} : \Sort{0} \\
   \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\mathit{Id}\;P \to \mathit{Id}\;P} \conv \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}
  {\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}
\]
The algorithm never decides where to apply \textsc{T-Conv}.
As described in \S\ref{sec:algorithm}, conversion is hidden in the call to \textsc{IsDefEq}, which runs only where two types are compared.

\paragraph{Exercises.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=\arabic*.]
  \item Prove $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{P \to Q \to P}}$.
    One answer is
    \[\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{\tLam{q}{Q}{p}}}}.\]
    The proof never uses $q$; this system allows hypotheses to go unused.
  \item Prove that implication is transitive:
    \[\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{R}{\Sort{0}}{(P \to Q) \to (Q \to R) \to P \to R}}}.\]
    One answer ends in $\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{g}{Q \to R}{\tLam{p}{P}{g\;(f\;p)}}}$; it uses the application case twice.
  \item Explain why $\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h\;h}}$ is rejected, and at which line of Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer}.
\end{enumerate}
Running \textsc{Infer} on these by hand, as in the examples above, is a good check of one's understanding of the algorithm.

\section{Inductive Types: From Natural Numbers to Equality}
\label{sec:inductive}

So far the only types are universes and $\Pi$ types.
This is enough for propositional logic, but not for mathematics: there are no numbers to reason about, and no way to state that two things are equal.
Lean provides both through a single mechanism, \emph{inductive types}.
We start with the natural numbers and ask two questions: how do we compute with them, and how do we prove things about them?
The answers turn out to be the same constant, the \emph{recursor} (\S\ref{sec:nat}).
We then generalize step by step, to more constructors (\S\ref{sec:tree}), and to parameters and indices (\S\ref{sec:list}),
and arrive at a procedure that works for any inductive declaration (\S\ref{sec:inductive-decl}).
Finally, we will see that even equality is an inductive type (\S\ref{sec:eq}).

\subsection{Constants and Definitions}
\label{sec:constants}

First we need a way to add named objects to the kernel.
Terms gain \emph{constants} $c$:
\[
t, A, B ::= \cdots \mid c
\]
A \emph{signature} $\Sigma$ lists the constants.
Each entry either declares a constant with its type, written $c : C$, or also gives it a body, written $c : C \mathrel{:=} t$; the latter are \emph{definitions}.
For example, $\Nat : \Sort{1}$ below is a declaration, and $\add$ in \S\ref{sec:nat} is a definition.
Before an entry is added, its type is checked to be a type in the empty context, and its body, if any, is checked against that type, as Lean does for each \texttt{def}.

The signature is used in two ways.
First, a constant has the type the signature gives it:
\[
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma} \\ (c : C) \in \Sigma}{\Gamma \vdash c : C}\rulename{T-Const}
\]
where $(c : C) \in \Sigma$ covers both declarations and definitions.
Second, a definition can be \emph{unfolded}: the constant is replaced by its body.
This computation step is called \emph{$\delta$-reduction}:
\[
c \deltared t \qquad \text{if } (c : C \mathrel{:=} t) \in \Sigma.
\]
For example, $\add\;2\;1 \deltared (\tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\cdots}})\;2\;1$, after which $\beta$-reduction continues.
A declared constant without a body, such as $\Nat$ or $\zero$, never $\delta$-reduces.
Like $\beta$, the step may be applied to any subterm.

Constants are not variables: they are never bound, so $\FV(c) = \emptyset$ and substitution leaves them unchanged.
Reduction now consists of $\beta$, $\delta$, and the $\iota$-rules introduced below, and conversion (\S\ref{sec:conversion}) is taken with respect to all three.

\subsection{Natural Numbers: Recursion and Induction}
\label{sec:nat}

In Lean, the natural numbers are declared as
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Nat where
  | zero : Nat
  | succ (n : Nat) : Nat
\end{lstlisting}
The declaration says that every natural number is built in one of two ways: it is $\zero$, or it is $\tsucc\;n$, the successor of a natural number $n$.
For example, $2$ is $\tsucc\;(\tsucc\;\zero)$.
In our kernel, the declaration adds three constants without bodies:
\[
\Nat : \Sort{1}, \qquad \zero : \Nat, \qquad \tsucc : \Nat \to \Nat.
\]
$\zero$ and $\tsucc$ are called \emph{constructors}.
They build values but never compute: $\tsucc\;(\tsucc\;\zero)$ is already in normal form, and it \emph{is} the number $2$.
We write $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ for $\zero$, $\tsucc\;\zero$, $\tsucc\;(\tsucc\;\zero)$, and so on.

This gives us numbers, but nothing to do with them.
A function such as addition must look at a number and act differently on $\zero$ and on $\tsucc\;n$, and our terms have no way to do that yet.

\paragraph{Computing: addition.}
How should addition be defined?
It can be defined by recursion on the second argument:
\[
\add\;m\;\zero = m, \qquad \add\;m\;(\tsucc\;k) = \tsucc\;(\add\;m\;k).
\]
Look at the shape of this definition.
For a fixed $m$, the function $\add\;m$ is determined by two pieces of data:
its value on $\zero$, which is $m$, and a way to turn its value $r$ on $k$ into its value on $\tsucc\;k$, which is $\tsucc\;r$.
Every function $f : \Nat \to C$ defined by recursion of this kind, called \emph{structural recursion}, has the same shape:
\[
f\;\zero = z, \qquad f\;(\tsucc\;k) = s\;k\;(f\;k),
\]
for some $z : C$ and $s : \Nat \to C \to C$; the step $s$ receives both $k$ and the result $f\;k$ of the recursive call.
So we add one constant that builds $f$ from $z$ and $s$, once and for all:
\[
\mathsf{rec}_C : C \to (\Nat \to C \to C) \to \Nat \to C,
\]
together with two computation rules, called \emph{$\iota$-rules}, which are exactly the equations above:
\[
\mathsf{rec}_C\;z\;s\;\zero \;\iotared\; z,
\qquad
\mathsf{rec}_C\;z\;s\;(\tsucc\;n) \;\iotared\; s\;n\;(\mathsf{rec}_C\;z\;s\;n).
\]
Addition is now an ordinary, non-recursive definition:
\[
\add : \Nat \to \Nat \to \Nat \mathrel{:=} \tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;m\;s\;n}},
\qquad
s = \tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;r}}.
\]
We write $m + n$ for $\add\;m\;n$.
The kernel computes $2 + 1$ with $\delta$, $\beta$, and $\iota$ steps only:
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}l}
2 + 1
&\to_{\delta\beta} \mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;2\;s\;(\tsucc\;0)
\;\iotared\; s\;0\;(\mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;2\;s\;0) \\
&\to_{\beta} \tsucc\;(\mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;2\;s\;0)
\;\iotared\; \tsucc\;2 = 3.
\end{array}
\]
Other functions follow the same pattern. Doubling, with $\mathit{double}\;(\tsucc\;k) = \tsucc\;(\tsucc\;(\mathit{double}\;k))$, is
\[
\mathit{double} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{n}{\Nat}{\mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;\zero\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;(\tsucc\;r)}})\;n},
\]
and $\mathit{double}\;2 \to \tsucc\;(\tsucc\;(\mathit{double}\;1)) \to \tsucc^4\;(\mathit{double}\;0) \to \tsucc^4\;\zero = 4$.

The interesting point is that no new recursion mechanism is needed.
The constants of the inductive type, together with $\mathsf{rec}_C$ and its two rules, are enough to express every structurally recursive function on $\Nat$.
And unlike general recursion, this one always terminates: each $\iota$-step removes one $\tsucc$ from the argument.

\paragraph{Proving: induction.}
Now consider proofs.
To prove that a property $P\;n$ holds for every $n$, where $P : \Nat \to \Sort{0}$, mathematics uses induction:
prove the \emph{base case} $P\;\zero$, and the \emph{step} $\tPi{k}{\Nat}{P\;k \to P\;(\tsucc\;k)}$, whose argument $P\;k$ is the \emph{induction hypothesis}.
Through Curry--Howard, a proof of $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{P\;n}$ is a function $f$ that takes $n$ and returns a proof of $P\;n$.
How do we build such an $f$ from $\mathit{base} : P\;\zero$ and $\mathit{step}$?
For $3$, the proof is $\mathit{step}\;2\;(\mathit{step}\;1\;(\mathit{step}\;0\;\mathit{base}))$, and in general
\[
f\;\zero = \mathit{base}, \qquad f\;(\tsucc\;k) = \mathit{step}\;k\;(f\;k).
\]
This is a structurally recursive function again, with exactly the shape of $\add$ above: $z = \mathit{base}$ and $s = \mathit{step}$.
Induction is recursion that returns proofs.

There is one difference.
For $\add$, the result type $C$ was the same for every $n$.
Here it depends on $n$: $f\;\zero : P\;\zero$, $f\;1 : P\;1$, and so on.
So $\mathsf{rec}_C$, whose type mentions a fixed $C$, cannot express induction as it stands.

\paragraph{One recursor for both.}
Putting the two cases side by side shows what to generalize:
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
& \textbf{Recursion} & \textbf{Induction} \\
\midrule
result for $n$ & $C$ & $P\;n$ \\
case $\zero$ & $z : C$ & $\mathit{base} : P\;\zero$ \\
case $\tsucc$ & $s : \tPi{k}{\Nat}{C \to C}$ & $\mathit{step} : \tPi{k}{\Nat}{P\;k \to P\;(\tsucc\;k)}$ \\
result & $\Nat \to C$ & $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{P\;n}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The left column is the special case of the right column in which $P\;n$ is the same type $C$ for every $n$.
So we take the right column, with $P$ replaced by an arbitrary function $M : \Nat \to \Sort{u}$ that gives the type of the result for each $n$.
This function is called the \emph{motive}.
The result is the \emph{recursor} $\NatRec{u}$ of Fig.~\ref{fig:nat}.
Its arguments are the motive, one \emph{minor premise} for each constructor, and finally the number $n$ to recurse on, called the \emph{major premise}.
Its $\iota$-rules are those of $\mathsf{rec}_C$.
As in Lean, where the recursor is \texttt{Nat.rec.\{u\}}, there is one recursor for each universe level; since we have no universe polymorphism, the level is a subscript.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\;:\;}l@{\qquad}l@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{Constant and type}} & \textbf{Lean} \\
\midrule
$\Nat$ & $\Sort{1}$ & \texttt{Nat} \\
$\zero$ & $\Nat$ & \texttt{Nat.zero} \\
$\tsucc$ & $\Nat \to \Nat$ & \texttt{Nat.succ} \\
$\NatRec{u}$ & $\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\tPi{M}{\Nat \to \Sort{u}}{M\;\zero \to {}} \\ \quad (\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n \to M\;(\tsucc\;n)}) \to \tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n}\end{array}$ & \texttt{Nat.rec} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;\zero &\iotared& z \\
\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;(\tsucc\;n) &\iotared& s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n)
\end{array}
\]
\caption{The constants for natural numbers (top) and the $\iota$-rules of the recursor (bottom).}
\label{fig:nat}
\end{figure}

The one recursor does both jobs, depending on the motive.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Recursion.} With the constant motive $\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{C}$ at level $1$, the type of $\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{C})$ is convertible to the type of $\mathsf{rec}_C$.
    So $\mathsf{rec}_C$ is just $\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{C})$, and from now on
    \[
    \add \mathrel{:=} \tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;m\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;r}})\;n}},
    \]
    which is the definition in \texttt{examples/zero-add.leanmini}.
  \item \emph{Induction.} With a predicate $M : \Nat \to \Sort{0}$ at level $0$, the type of $\NatRec{0}$ is the induction principle
    \[
    M\;\zero \to (\forall n.\; M\;n \to M\;(\tsucc\;n)) \to \forall n.\; M\;n.
    \]
    Here the choice of $\imax$ (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}) is essential.
    The conclusion $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n}$ has type $\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}$, so ``$M\;n$ for every $n$'' is a proposition although $\Nat$ lives in $\Sort{1}$.
    With $\max$, it would live in $\Sort{1}$, and statements about numbers would not be propositions.
\end{itemize}

The type of $\NatRec{u}$ is not arbitrary: it can be read off the declaration of $\Nat$.
There is one minor premise per constructor.
Each minor premise takes the constructor's arguments, plus one induction hypothesis for each argument whose type is $\Nat$ itself (a \emph{recursive} argument),
and returns the motive applied to the constructor.
$\zero$ has no arguments, so its case is just $M\;\zero$; $\tsucc$ has one recursive argument $n$, so its case is $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n \to M\;(\tsucc\;n)}$.
The rest of this section applies this recipe to more and more general declarations.

\subsection{More Constructors: Trees}
\label{sec:tree}

$\Nat$ has two constructors, and only one of them has a recursive argument.
Consider a type with three constructors:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Tree where
  | leaf   : Tree
  | node   : Tree -> Tree
  | branch : Tree -> Tree -> Tree
\end{lstlisting}
For example, $\mathsf{branch}\;(\mathsf{node}\;\mathsf{leaf})\;\mathsf{leaf}$ is a tree with four constructors.
To build $M\;t$ for every tree $t$, where $M : \mathsf{Tree} \to \Sort{v}$, the recipe asks for one case per constructor,
and each argument of type $\mathsf{Tree}$ contributes one hypothesis:
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\;:\;}l}
m_{\mathsf{leaf}} & M\;\mathsf{leaf} \\
m_{\mathsf{node}} & \tPi{t}{\mathsf{Tree}}{M\;t \to M\;(\mathsf{node}\;t)} \\
m_{\mathsf{branch}} & \tPi{l}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tPi{r}{\mathsf{Tree}}{M\;l \to M\;r \to M\;(\mathsf{branch}\;l\;r)}}
\end{array}
\]
The recursor takes the motive, the three cases, and a tree:
\[
\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v : \tPi{M}{\mathsf{Tree} \to \Sort{v}}{\;
  M\;\mathsf{leaf} \to (\cdots_{\mathsf{node}}) \to (\cdots_{\mathsf{branch}}) \to \tPi{t}{\mathsf{Tree}}{M\;t}},
\]
where the dots stand for the types of $m_{\mathsf{node}}$ and $m_{\mathsf{branch}}$.
Compared with $\NatRec{v}$, only the number of cases and the number of hypotheses per case have changed.
Writing $R$ for the partial application $\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v\;M\;m_{\mathsf{leaf}}\;m_{\mathsf{node}}\;m_{\mathsf{branch}}$,
the $\iota$-rules are
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
R\;\mathsf{leaf} &\iotared& m_{\mathsf{leaf}} \\
R\;(\mathsf{node}\;t) &\iotared& m_{\mathsf{node}}\;t\;(R\;t) \\
R\;(\mathsf{branch}\;l\;r) &\iotared& m_{\mathsf{branch}}\;l\;r\;(R\;l)\;(R\;r).
\end{array}
\]
Each rule selects the case for the constructor at the head of the major premise, and fills each hypothesis with a recursive call on the corresponding subtree.
For example, with $M = \tLam{\_}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\Nat}$ and the cases
\[
\begin{array}{l}
m_{\mathsf{leaf}} = 1, \qquad
m_{\mathsf{node}} = \tLam{t}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tLam{i}{\Nat}{1 + i}}, \\[2pt]
m_{\mathsf{branch}} = \tLam{l}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tLam{r}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tLam{i}{\Nat}{\tLam{j}{\Nat}{1 + i + j}}}},
\end{array}
\]
$R$ counts the constructors of a tree, and
\[
R\;(\mathsf{branch}\;(\mathsf{node}\;\mathsf{leaf})\;\mathsf{leaf})
\to 1 + R\;(\mathsf{node}\;\mathsf{leaf}) + R\;\mathsf{leaf}
\to 1 + (1 + R\;\mathsf{leaf}) + 1
\to 1 + (1 + 1) + 1 = 4.
\]
With $M$ a predicate ($v = 0$), the same recursor is structural induction on trees.
In general, a type with $n$ constructors gets a recursor with $n$ minor premises $m_1, \ldots, m_n$,
and the kernel needs no code specific to the type: it only needs to know, for each constructor, which case to pick and which arguments to recurse on.

\subsection{Parameters and Indices: Lists and Vectors}
\label{sec:list}

\paragraph{Parameters: lists.}

Next, consider lists.
A list of numbers is either empty or a number in front of a list of numbers, so we could declare a type $\mathsf{ListNat}$ with constructors $\mathsf{nil}$ and $\mathsf{cons} : \Nat \to \mathsf{ListNat} \to \mathsf{ListNat}$.
But then lists of trees would need another declaration, $\mathsf{ListTree}$, with the same constructors and a separate recursor, and so on for every element type.
It is better to make the element type an argument of the type itself:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive List (A : Sort 1) where
  | nil  : List A
  | cons : A -> List A -> List A
\end{lstlisting}
Now $\mathsf{List}\;\Nat$ and $\mathsf{List}\;\mathsf{Tree}$ are two instances of one declaration.
The declaration adds
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\mathsf{List} : \Sort{1} \to \Sort{1}, \qquad
\mathsf{nil} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\mathsf{List}\;A}, \\
\mathsf{cons} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{A \to \mathsf{List}\;A \to \mathsf{List}\;A}.
\end{array}
\]
The constructors take $A$ as an explicit first argument.
For example, the one-element list $[5]$ is $\mathsf{cons}\;\Nat\;5\;(\mathsf{nil}\;\Nat)$.
Within one list, $A$ never changes: the tail of $\mathsf{cons}\;A\;a\;\mathit{as}$ is again a $\mathsf{List}\;A$.
An argument of the type that stays the same in every constructor and every recursive argument is called a \emph{parameter}.
Because it never changes, the recursor can take it once, before the motive, and treat it as fixed:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\mathsf{List.rec}_v : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tPi{M}{\mathsf{List}\;A \to \Sort{v}}{\;M\;(\mathsf{nil}\;A) \to {}}} \\
\qquad (\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{\mathit{as}}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{M\;\mathit{as} \to M\;(\mathsf{cons}\;A\;a\;\mathit{as})}}) \to \tPi{x}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{M\;x} \\[6pt]
\mathsf{List.rec}_v\;A\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;(\mathsf{nil}\;A') \;\iotared\; m_1 \\
\mathsf{List.rec}_v\;A\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;(\mathsf{cons}\;A'\;a\;\mathit{as}) \;\iotared\; m_2\;a\;\mathit{as}\;(\mathsf{List.rec}_v\;A\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;\mathit{as})
\end{array}
\]
Apart from the leading $A$, this is the recipe of \S\ref{sec:nat} once more:
$\mathsf{cons}$ has two arguments, of which only $\mathit{as}$ is recursive, so its case gets one induction hypothesis.
The rules ignore the parameter $A'$ stored in the constructor; in a well-typed term it is convertible to $A$.
For example, the length of a list is
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\mathit{length} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tLam{x}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{{}}} \\
\qquad \mathsf{List.rec}_1\;A\;(\tLam{\_}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{\Nat})\;\zero\;(\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{\mathit{as}}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;r}}})\;x.
\end{array}
\]

\paragraph{Indices: vectors.}
A $\mathsf{List}\;\Nat$ may have any length.
What if we want the length to be part of the type, so that $\mathsf{Vec}\;\Nat\;0$ and $\mathsf{Vec}\;\Nat\;2$ are different types?
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Vec (A : Sort 1) : Nat -> Sort 1 where
  | vnil  : Vec A 0
  | vcons : (n : Nat) -> A -> Vec A n -> Vec A (succ n)
\end{lstlisting}
The element type $A$ is still a parameter.
The length is not: $\mathsf{vnil}$ has length $0$, and $\mathsf{vcons}$ takes a vector of length $n$ and returns one of length $\tsucc\;n$.
An argument of the type that may differ between constructors, and between a constructor and its recursive arguments, is called an \emph{index}.
The constructors are
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\mathsf{vnil} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;\zero}, \\
\mathsf{vcons} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tPi{n}{\Nat}{A \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;(\tsucc\;n)}}.
\end{array}
\]
Because an index varies, the recursor cannot fix it in advance.
Instead, the motive takes it as an argument, $M : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n \to \Sort{v}}$, and the case for $\mathsf{vcons}$ is
\[
\tPi{n}{\Nat}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{\mathit{xs}}{\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n}{M\;n\;\mathit{xs} \to M\;(\tsucc\;n)\;(\mathsf{vcons}\;A\;n\;a\;\mathit{xs})}}}.
\]
The induction hypothesis is about a vector of length $n$, read off the type $\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n$ of the recursive argument,
and the conclusion is about one of length $\tsucc\;n$, read off the result type of the constructor.
\texttt{examples/generic-vec.leanmini} declares this type and checks a small term that uses it.

\subsection{The General Recipe}
\label{sec:inductive-decl}

In Lean, a user never writes recursors or $\iota$-rules.
The user writes an \texttt{inductive} declaration, and the kernel checks it and generates the type, the constructors, the recursor, and the rules,
following the recipe that \S\S\ref{sec:nat}--\ref{sec:list} applied by hand.
This subsection states that procedure for a single inductive type with parameters and indices.
Mutual and nested inductive types, which Lean also supports, are out of scope.

The procedure also answers a question that \textsc{T-Const} leaves open.
A constant without a body is an assumption: \textsc{T-Const} would accept $c : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$ just as readily as $\zero : \Nat$, and with it the system would be inconsistent.
The constants generated below are not arbitrary assumptions.
They are instances of a fixed schema, the inductive types of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, whose consistency is known~\cite{werner1994theorie}.

\paragraph{Telescopes.}
We write $(\vec{x} : \vec{A})$ for a sequence of bindings $(x_1 : A_1) \cdots (x_k : A_k)$ in which each $A_i$ may mention $x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}$,
$\tPi{\vec{x}}{\vec{A}}{B}$ for $\tPi{x_1}{A_1}{\cdots\,\tPi{x_k}{A_k}{B}}$, and $f\;\vec{x}$ for $f\;x_1 \cdots x_k$.
The length of $\vec{x}$ is written $|\vec{x}|$.

\paragraph{Declarations.}
A declaration introduces a type former $I$ and constructors $c_1, \ldots, c_n$:
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l@{\qquad}l}
I &:& \tPi{\vec{p}}{\vec{P}}{\tPi{\vec{\imath}}{\vec{J}}{\Sort{u}}} & \\
c_j &:& \tPi{\vec{p}}{\vec{P}}{\tPi{\vec{a}}{\vec{A}_j}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{t}_j}} & (j = 1, \ldots, n)
\end{array}
\]
The \emph{parameters} $\vec{p}$ are shared by all constructors and appear unchanged in every result type.
The \emph{indices} $\vec{\imath}$ may differ between constructors: the index terms $\vec{t}_j$ may mention $\vec{p}$ and the constructor's own arguments $\vec{a}$, which are called its \emph{fields}.
For the examples so far, with the leading $\Pi$ over the parameters omitted from the constructor types:
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Type former} & \textbf{Parameters} & \textbf{Indices} & \textbf{Constructors} \\
\midrule
$\Nat : \Sort{1}$ & none & none & $\zero : \Nat$, \\
& & & $\tsucc : \Nat \to \Nat$ \\
$\mathsf{Tree} : \Sort{1}$ & none & none & $\mathsf{leaf}$, $\mathsf{node}$, $\mathsf{branch}$ \\
$\mathsf{List} : \Sort{1} \to \Sort{1}$ & $(A : \Sort{1})$ & none & $\mathsf{nil} : \mathsf{List}\;A$, \\
& & & $\mathsf{cons} : A \to \mathsf{List}\;A \to \mathsf{List}\;A$ \\
$\mathsf{Vec} : \Sort{1} \to \Nat \to \Sort{1}$ & $(A : \Sort{1})$ & $(n : \Nat)$ & $\mathsf{vnil} : \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;\zero$, \\
& & & $\mathsf{vcons} : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{A \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;(\tsucc\;n)}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\paragraph{Acceptance.}
The kernel accepts a declaration only if the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item The type of $I$ is a type in the current signature.
  \item With $I$ added to the signature, each constructor type is a type, and it ends in $I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{t}_j$, where $\vec{p}$ are exactly the parameters in order and $I$ does not occur in $\vec{t}_j$.
  \item \emph{Strict positivity.} Each field type either does not mention $I$, or has the form $\tPi{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{s}}$ where $I$ occurs neither in $\vec{B}$ nor in $\vec{s}$.
    A field of the second form is \emph{recursive}.
  \item \emph{Universes.} If $u \ge 1$, each field type lies in some $\Sort{w}$ with $w \le u$. If $u = 0$, there is no condition.
\end{enumerate}
Condition~2 lets the recursor treat the parameters uniformly.
Condition~3 rules out declarations such as
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Bad where
  | mk : (Bad -> False) -> Bad
\end{lstlisting}
whose field mentions \texttt{Bad} to the left of an arrow.
Case analysis on \texttt{Bad} would let one define $f : \mathtt{Bad} \to \mathtt{False}$ by $f\;(\mathtt{mk}\;g) = g\;(\mathtt{mk}\;g)$.
Then $f\;(\mathtt{mk}\;f)$ is a closed term of type $\mathtt{False}$, and it reduces to itself, so it has no normal form.
For a type \texttt{Tree} under declaration, some field types and their status are:
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Field type} & \textbf{Status} & \textbf{Reason} \\
\midrule
$\Nat$ & accepted, not recursive & does not mention \texttt{Tree} \\
$\mathsf{Tree}$ & accepted, recursive & induction hypothesis $M\;a_k$ \\
$\Nat \to \mathsf{Tree}$ & accepted, recursive & produces trees; hypothesis $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;(a_k\;n)}$ \\
$\mathsf{Tree} \to \Nat$ & rejected & \texttt{Tree} to the left of an arrow \\
$\mathsf{List}\;\mathsf{Tree}$ & rejected here & nested occurrence; Lean accepts it, but this is out of scope \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
A field of type $\Nat \to \mathsf{Tree}$ is a tree with infinitely many children, one for each number;
the recursor can still recurse into each child $a_k\;n$.
A field of type $\mathsf{Tree} \to \Nat$ consumes trees instead of containing them, and it is the shape that makes \texttt{Bad} paradoxical.
Condition~4 prevents a type from containing a larger universe.
Without it, a declaration $T : \Sort{1}$ with a constructor $\mathtt{mk} : \Sort{1} \to T$ would place a copy of all of $\Sort{1}$ inside $\Sort{1}$,
which is the self-containment that \S\ref{sec:typetype} shows to be inconsistent.
For $u = 0$ no condition is needed, because $\Sort{0}$ is impredicative (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).

\paragraph{The recursor.}
For an accepted declaration, the kernel generates a recursor $I.\mathsf{rec}_v$ for each admissible level $v$ (see below):
\[
I.\mathsf{rec}_v :
\tPi{\vec{p}}{\vec{P}}{\;
\tPi{M}{(\tPi{\vec{\imath}}{\vec{J}}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{\imath} \to \Sort{v}})}{\;
\tPi{m_1}{C_1}{\cdots\,\tPi{m_n}{C_n}{\;
\tPi{\vec{\imath}}{\vec{J}}{\tPi{x}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{\imath}}{M\;\vec{\imath}\;x}}}}}}.
\]
The parameters come first and stay fixed, as for lists; the motive takes the indices and the element, as for vectors.
The minor premise $C_j$ asks for the case of constructor $c_j$: given its fields and an induction hypothesis for each recursive field, build $M$ for $c_j$ applied to those fields:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
C_j = \tPi{\vec{a}}{\vec{A}_j}{\;\tPi{\vec{h}}{\vec{H}_j}{\;M\;\vec{t}_j\;(c_j\;\vec{p}\;\vec{a})}}, \\[4pt]
H_{j,k} = \tPi{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{M\;\vec{s}\;(a_k\;\vec{y})}
\quad\text{for each recursive field } a_k : \tPi{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{s}}.
\end{array}
\]
The final arguments are the indices and the element $x$ itself, the major premise.

\paragraph{The rules.}
For each constructor, the kernel generates one $\iota$-rule, which applies the minor premise to the fields and to the induction hypotheses, computed by recursive calls:
\[
I.\mathsf{rec}_v\;\vec{p}\;M\;\vec{m}\;\vec{\imath}\;(c_j\;\vec{p}\,'\;\vec{a}) \;\iotared\; m_j\;\vec{a}\;\vec{h},
\qquad
h_k = \tLam{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{I.\mathsf{rec}_v\;\vec{p}\;M\;\vec{m}\;\vec{s}\;(a_k\;\vec{y})}.
\]
As data for Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf} (\S\ref{sec:iota-data}), the major premise is at position $|\vec{p}| + n + |\vec{\imath}| + 2$,
the constructor has $|\vec{p}|$ parameters and $|\vec{a}|$ fields,
and the right-hand side is $\lambda \vec{p}\,M\,\vec{m}\,\vec{\imath}.\;\lambda \vec{a}.\; m_j\;\vec{a}\;\vec{h}$.
In a well-typed redex, $\vec{p}\,'$ is convertible to $\vec{p}$, so the rule ignores it, as the rules for lists ignore $A'$.
For $\Nat$, $\mathsf{Tree}$, $\mathsf{List}$, and $\mathsf{Vec}$, the procedure produces exactly the recursors and rules of \S\S\ref{sec:nat}--\ref{sec:list},
and the recursor types agree with the ones Lean 4 generates, up to the names of bound variables and implicit arguments.

\paragraph{Eliminating from propositions.}
If $u \ge 1$, the recursor is generated for every level $v$.
If $u = 0$, so that $I$ is a proposition, the recursor is generated only for $v = 0$, unless $I$ is a \emph{subsingleton}:
it has at most one constructor, and each field either is a proof (its type lies in $\Sort{0}$) or occurs among the index terms $\vec{t}_j$.
The restriction keeps data from depending on which proof of a proposition was given.
For example, $P \vee Q$ has two constructors, so a function from proofs of $P \vee Q$ into $\Nat$ could return $0$ for one and $1$ for the other.
Lean's \texttt{Or.rec} and \texttt{Exists.rec} therefore eliminate only into $\mathsf{Prop}$,
while \texttt{And.rec} and \texttt{Eq.rec} eliminate into every universe: \texttt{And} has one constructor whose fields are proofs, and \texttt{Eq} (\S\ref{sec:eq}) has one constructor with no fields.

So the kernel's rules stay fixed while the signature grows: one generic procedure turns each declaration into signature entries, and a single reduction function runs their rules (\S\ref{sec:iota-data}).

\subsection{Equality Is an Inductive Type Too}
\label{sec:eq}

To state facts about numbers, such as $0 + n = n$, we need a way to say that two things are equal.
One might expect equality to be a primitive of the kernel.
Surprisingly, it is just another inductive type:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Eq {A : Sort u} (a : A) : A -> Prop where
  | refl : Eq a a
\end{lstlisting}
For $a, b : A$, the type $\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$ is the proposition that $a$ and $b$ are equal; when $A$ is $\Nat$ we write it $a = b$.
In the terms of \S\ref{sec:inductive-decl}, $A$ and $a$ are parameters and $b$ is an index:
\[
\Eq{u} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{A \to A \to \Sort{0}}, \qquad
\refl{u} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;a}}.
\]
The only constructor $\refl{u}$ has no fields, and its index term is $a$: it can only prove equations whose two sides are the same.
So $\Eq{}$ is an \emph{inductive family} like $\mathsf{Vec}$, not a single type.

The general recipe gives its recursor.
Because $b$ is an index, the motive takes $b$ and the proof $h : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$, and there is one minor premise, for $\refl{u}$, with no fields and no hypotheses:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\EqRecDep{u,v} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{M}{(\tPi{b}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \to \Sort{v}})}{{}}}} \\
\qquad M\;a\;(\refl{u}\;A\;a) \to \tPi{b}{A}{\tPi{h}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b}{M\;b\;h}} \\[6pt]
\EqRecDep{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A'\;c) \;\iotared\; m.
\end{array}
\]
$\Eq{}$ is a subsingleton, so $v$ is arbitrary.
Read logically, the recursor says: if something holds in the case where the two sides are identical, then it holds whenever we have a proof that they are equal.
Most uses need only the non-dependent version $\EqRec{u,v}$, whose motive ignores the proof.
It is a definition built from $\EqRecDep{u,v}$,
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\EqRec{u,v} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{M}{A \to \Sort{v}}{\tLam{m}{M\;a}{\tLam{b}{A}{\tLam{h}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b}{{}}}}}}} \\
\qquad \EqRecDep{u,v}\;A\;a\;(\tLam{b'}{A}{\tLam{\_}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b'}{M\;b'}})\;m\;b\;h,
\end{array}
\]
and Fig.~\ref{fig:eq} summarizes the constants.
$\EqRec{u,v}$ is Leibniz's principle: if $a = b$, then whatever holds of $a$ holds of $b$.
It \emph{transports} $m : M\;a$ along a proof of $a = b$ to $M\;b$, and its rule says that transporting along $\refl{}$ does nothing.
In a well-typed redex, $b$ and $c$ are both convertible to $a$, so the rules can ignore them.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\;:\;}l@{\qquad}l@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{Constant and type}} & \textbf{Lean} \\
\midrule
$\Eq{u}$ & $\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{A \to A \to \Sort{0}}$ & \texttt{Eq} \\
$\refl{u}$ & $\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;a}}$ & \texttt{Eq.refl} \\
$\EqRecDep{u,v}$ & $\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{M}{(\tPi{b}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \to \Sort{v}})}{{}}}} \\ \quad M\;a\;(\refl{u}\;A\;a) \to \tPi{b}{A}{\tPi{h}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b}{M\;b\;h}}\end{array}$ & \texttt{Eq.rec} \\
$\EqRec{u,v}$ & $\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{M}{A \to \Sort{v}}{{}}}} \\ \quad M\;a \to \tPi{b}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \to M\;b}\end{array}$ & \texttt{Eq.ndrec} (definition) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
\EqRecDep{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A\;c) &\iotared& m \\
\EqRec{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A\;c) &\to_{\delta\beta\iota}& m
\end{array}
\]
\caption{The constants for equality and their computation rules. The rule for $\EqRec{u,v}$ is derived from its definition by $\delta$, $\beta$, and the rule for $\EqRecDep{u,v}$.}
\label{fig:eq}
\end{figure}

For example, suppose $P : \Nat \to \Sort{0}$, $a, b : \Nat$, $h : a = b$, and $\mathit{pa} : P\;a$.
Choosing the motive $M = P$ gives
\[
\EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;a\;P\;\mathit{pa}\;b\;h \;:\; P\;b.
\]
This one line is the logical content of rewriting: a fact about $a$ becomes a fact about $b$.
The \texttt{rw} tactic of \S\ref{sec:tactics} builds such terms automatically.

In Lean, the type argument of \texttt{Eq} is \emph{implicit}, written \texttt{\{A\}} above, and the elaborator fills it in.
Our kernel sees only fully explicit terms, so we write every argument; filling them in is the job of the layer above the kernel (\S\ref{sec:tactics}).

\paragraph{Definitional versus propositional equality.}
There are now two notions of equality.
Definitional equality $\conv$ is decided by the kernel by computation; propositional equality $\Eq{}$ is a type, whose proofs may require reasoning.
The constructor $\refl{}$ connects them: by \textsc{T-Conv}, $\refl{u}\;A\;a : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$ whenever $a \conv b$.
For example, with the definition of $\add$ from \S\ref{sec:nat} and $s$ its step,
\[
n + 0 \;\to_{\delta\beta}\; \NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;n\;s\;\zero \;\iotared\; n,
\]
so $\refl{1}\;\Nat\;n : n + 0 = n$, and Lean proves this by \texttt{rfl}.
In contrast,
\[
0 + n \;\to_{\delta\beta}\; \NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;0\;s\;n
\]
is stuck: $n$ is a variable, and the $\iota$-rules fire only on $\zero$ and $\tsucc$.
So $0 + n = n$ is not provable by $\refl{}$ and needs induction.

\subsection{Example: $0 + n = n$}
\label{sec:zero-add}

We prove $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}$ by induction, using $\NatRec{0}$ with the motive $M_0 = \tLam{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Base.} We need $M_0\;0$, which is convertible to $0 + 0 = 0$. Since $0 + 0$ computes to $0$, the term $\refl{1}\;\Nat\;0$ works.
  \item \emph{Step.} Given $k : \Nat$ and $\mathit{ih} : 0 + k = k$, we need $M_0\;(\tsucc\;k)$, that is, $0 + \tsucc\;k = \tsucc\;k$.
    By the second $\iota$-rule, $0 + \tsucc\;k$ computes to $\tsucc\;(0 + k)$, so it suffices to prove $\tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;k$.
    We start from $\refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\tsucc\;(0 + k))$ and transport it along $\mathit{ih}$ with the motive $N = \tLam{b}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;b}$,
    which replaces the second $0 + k$ by $k$:
    \[
    \mathit{step} = \tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{0 + k = k}{
      \EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;(0 + k)\;N\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\tsucc\;(0 + k)))\;k\;\mathit{ih}}}.
    \]
\end{itemize}
The proof is
\[
\mathit{zero\_add} = \NatRec{0}\;M_0\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;0)\;\mathit{step} \;:\; \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}.
\]
The kernel checks it with Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer}.
Each argument is checked against the corresponding part of the type of $\NatRec{0}$, instantiated with $M_0$, and every comparison succeeds after normalization.
Writing such terms by hand is tedious, and finding the right motive is the hard part; tactics (\S\ref{sec:tactics}) automate both.

\subsection{Changes to the Kernel}

\textsc{Infer} gains a case for constants, which looks up the type in $\Sigma$ (\textsc{T-Const}).
\textsc{Check} is unchanged; only \textsc{Whnf}, and through it \textsc{IsDefEq}, learns the new $\delta$- and $\iota$-steps.
\S\ref{sec:iota-data} shows how a single \textsc{Whnf} handles every inductive type,
and \S\ref{sec:properties} discusses what inductive types change in the metatheory.


\section{Tactics: Building Proof Terms Interactively}
\label{sec:tactics}

Lean users rarely write terms like $\mathit{zero\_add}$ by hand.
They write a tactic script instead:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
theorem zero_add (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, ih]
\end{lstlisting}
Each tactic is a small program that builds part of the proof term.
Tactics run outside the kernel.
Their output is an ordinary term, which the kernel checks with Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} like any other term.
This section shows how the common tactics construct terms in our system.

\subsection{Goals and Proof States}

A \emph{goal} $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle$ asks for a term of type $T$ in the context $\Gamma$.
The \emph{hole} $\hole{m}$ stands for the term still to be found; Lean calls it a \emph{metavariable}.
A \emph{proof state} is a list of goals together with a \emph{partial proof term}, a term that may contain holes.

To prove $T$, we start from the partial term $\hole{0}$ and the single goal $\langle \cdot \vdash \hole{0} : T \rangle$.
A tactic works on the first goal $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle$.
It \emph{assigns} to $\hole{m}$ a term that may contain fresh holes, and replaces the goal by one new goal for each fresh hole.
When no goals remain, the partial term contains no holes, and the kernel checks it against $T$.
A hole may sit under binders, as $\hole{1}$ does in $\tLam{x}{A}{\hole{1}}$, and the term that fills it may use those bound variables.
That is why each goal carries its own context.

Each tactic must make sure that its assignment has type $T$ in $\Gamma$, assuming each fresh hole is later filled with a term of the type its goal states.
We write $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \leadsto \text{new goals}$, followed by the assignment.

\paragraph{A first example.}
The script of \texttt{examples/identity.leanmini} proves the opening example of \S\ref{sec:curry-howard}:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
goal forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P
intro P
intro p
exact p
qed
\end{lstlisting}
The proof state evolves as follows; each line shows the goals and the assignment made by the tactic.
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\qquad}l@{\qquad}l}
\textbf{Tactic} & \textbf{Goals afterwards} & \textbf{Assignment} \\
\text{(start)} & \langle \cdot \vdash \hole{0} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} \rangle & \\
\texttt{intro P} & \langle P : \Sort{0} \vdash \hole{1} : P \to P \rangle & \hole{0} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\hole{1}} \\
\texttt{intro p} & \langle P : \Sort{0}, p : P \vdash \hole{2} : P \rangle & \hole{1} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{p}{P}{\hole{2}} \\
\texttt{exact p} & \text{none} & \hole{2} \mathrel{:=} p
\end{array}
\]
Substituting the assignments into $\hole{0}$ gives $\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}$, the term we wrote by hand,
and \texttt{qed} sends it to $\textsc{Check}$.
A list of goals alone would not be enough: after \texttt{intro p}, the goal $P$ does not remember that its solution must be wrapped in two $\lambda$s.
The partial term records exactly that.

\subsection{Basic Tactics}

\paragraph{\texttt{intro x}.}
If $T$ normalizes to a $\Pi$ type, the tactic moves its argument into the context:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : \tPi{y}{A}{B} \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma, x : A \vdash \hole{1} : \subst{B}{y}{x} \rangle,
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{x}{A}{\hole{1}}.
\]
The assignment has the right type by \textsc{T-Lam}.
The name $x$ must not be in $\dom(\Gamma)$; otherwise the new assumption would shadow an existing one, which makes the kernel unsound (\S\ref{sec:capture}), so the tactic must rename it.

\paragraph{\texttt{exact t}.}
The tactic closes the goal with a given term:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \text{no goals},
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} t,
\]
after running $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma, t, T)$ itself.
The kernel would reject an ill-typed $t$ at the end anyway; checking early only gives a better error message.

\paragraph{\texttt{apply f}.}
If $f$ has type $A_1 \to \cdots \to A_n \to B$ with $B \conv T$, the tactic leaves the arguments as new goals:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{1} : A_1 \rangle, \ldots, \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{n} : A_n \rangle,
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} f\;\hole{1} \cdots \hole{n}.
\]
The assignment has type $B$ by $n$ uses of \textsc{T-App}, and type $T$ by \textsc{T-Conv}.
When the type of $f$ is a dependent $\Pi$, later $A_i$ and $B$ mention earlier arguments, and the tactic must find those arguments by matching $B$ against $T$.
Lean does this by \emph{unification}, solving for metavariables.
Our restricted version handles only non-dependent arrows.

For example, transitivity of implication (the second exercise of \S\ref{sec:examples}) works backwards from the conclusion:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
goal forall (P : Sort 0), forall (Q : Sort 0), forall (R : Sort 0), (P -> Q) -> (Q -> R) -> P -> R
intro P
intro Q
intro R
intro f
intro g
intro p
apply g
apply f
exact p
qed
\end{lstlisting}
After the six \texttt{intro}s the goal is $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{6} : R \rangle$ with $\Gamma = P, Q, R : \Sort{0},\; f : P \to Q,\; g : Q \to R,\; p : P$.
No hypothesis has type $R$, so \texttt{exact} cannot close it, but $g$ ends in $R$:
\texttt{apply g} assigns $\hole{6} \mathrel{:=} g\;\hole{7}$ and leaves $\hole{7} : Q$.
Likewise \texttt{apply f} assigns $\hole{7} \mathrel{:=} f\;\hole{8}$ and leaves $\hole{8} : P$, which \texttt{exact p} closes.
The body of the resulting term is $g\;(f\;p)$.
Note the difference between the two tactics: \texttt{exact g} fails, because $g$ has type $Q \to R$, not $R$,
whereas \texttt{apply g} turns the missing argument of $g$ into a new goal.

\paragraph{\texttt{change T'}.}
The tactic replaces the goal by a definitionally equal one:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{1} : T' \rangle,
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \hole{1},
\]
provided $T'$ is a type and $T' \conv T$.
It adds nothing to the term; it only changes how the goal is displayed, and \textsc{T-Conv} justifies it.
\texttt{change} is needed because \texttt{rw} (below) finds subterms only up to $\alpha$-equivalence:
a subterm that appears only after computation must first be exposed with \texttt{change}, as in the example of \S\ref{sec:zero-add-tactics}.

\paragraph{\texttt{rfl}.}
If $T$ normalizes to $\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$ with $a \conv b$, the tactic closes the goal:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \rangle \;\leadsto\; \text{no goals},
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \refl{u}\;A\;a.
\]
The assignment has type $\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;a$, which is convertible to the goal.
So \texttt{rfl} proves exactly the equations that hold by definitional equality (\S\ref{sec:eq}).

\subsection{Induction}

Let $n : \Nat$ be a variable in $\Gamma$, and let $\Gamma \vdash T : \Sort{u}$.
The tactic \texttt{induction n} abstracts $n$ in the goal to form the motive, and produces one goal per constructor:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle
\;\leadsto\;
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{z} : \subst{T}{n}{\zero} \rangle,\;
\langle \Gamma, k : \Nat, \mathit{ih} : \subst{T}{n}{k} \vdash \hole{s} : \subst{T}{n}{\tsucc\;k} \rangle, \\[4pt]
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \NatRec{u}\;(\tLam{z}{\Nat}{\subst{T}{n}{z}})\;\hole{z}\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{\subst{T}{n}{k}}{\hole{s}}})\;n.
\end{array}
\]
With the motive $M = \tLam{z}{\Nat}{\subst{T}{n}{z}}$, the type of $\NatRec{u}\;M$ asks for $M\;\zero$ and $\tPi{k}{\Nat}{M\;k \to M\;(\tsucc\;k)}$, and the result has type $M\;n$.
These are convertible to the types of the two goals and to $T$, by $\beta$.
The construction is correct only if the names are fresh, the level $u$ is right, and no other hypothesis mentions $n$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item The motive binds a fresh name $z$, not $n$: since $n$ is already in $\Gamma$, writing $\tLam{n}{\Nat}{T}$ would shadow it, which is the pitfall of \S\ref{sec:capture}.
    Likewise $k$ and $\mathit{ih}$ must be fresh.
  \item The level $u$ of the motive comes from the type of the goal, found by \textsc{InferSort}. For a proposition it is $0$, and $\NatRec{0}$ is induction.
  \item If another hypothesis mentions $n$, for example $h : n = 2$, the new goals still contain $h$ about the original $n$, and $\mathit{ih}$ says nothing about it.
    The goals are then correct but may be unprovable.
    Lean's \texttt{induction} first moves such hypotheses into the goal (it \emph{reverts} them), so that they are part of the motive.
    Our version requires that no other hypothesis mentions $n$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Rewriting}

Let $h : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$, and let the goal $T$ be a proposition.
The tactic \texttt{rw [h]} replaces $a$ by $b$ in the goal in four steps.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Abstract.} Choose a fresh $x$ and let $C$ be $T$ with every occurrence of $a$ replaced by $x$.
    Occurrences are found up to $\alpha$-equivalence, not up to conversion,
    and an occurrence under a binder that binds a free variable of $a$ is skipped, since there it denotes something else.
  \item \emph{Check the motive.} Check that $\Gamma, x : A \vdash C : \Sort{0}$. This can fail, as shown below.
  \item \emph{Build the term.} The new goal is $\subst{C}{x}{b}$, the goal with $a$ replaced by $b$:
    \[
    \begin{array}{l}
    \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{1} : \subst{C}{x}{b} \rangle, \\[4pt]
    \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \EqRec{u,0}\;A\;a\;(\tLam{x}{A}{C \to T})\;(\tLam{p}{T}{p})\;b\;h\;\hole{1}.
    \end{array}
    \]
  \item \emph{Try \texttt{rfl}.} Like Lean, close the new goal by \texttt{rfl} if possible.
\end{enumerate}
To see that the assignment has type $T$, write $N = \tLam{x}{A}{C \to T}$ for the motive.
Since $\subst{C}{x}{a} = T$, the term $N\;a$ is convertible to $T \to T$, which the identity $\tLam{p}{T}{p}$ inhabits.
Transport along $h$ then gives $N\;b$, which is convertible to $\subst{C}{x}{b} \to T$, and applying it to $\hole{1}$ gives $T$.
Lean builds a different term, \texttt{Eq.mpr (congrArg (fun x => C) h)}, from the same idea.

\paragraph{When the motive is ill typed.}
Abstracting $a$ can break the goal.
Let $\Gamma = n : \Nat,\; h : n = 2,\; q : n = 0$, and suppose we run \texttt{rw [h]} on the goal $\Eq{0}\;(n = 0)\;q\;q$, a statement about the proof $q$.
Abstracting $n$ gives $C = \Eq{0}\;(x = 0)\;q\;q$, which is ill typed: $q$ has type $n = 0$, not $x = 0$, and $q$ itself cannot be abstracted.
Step~2 fails, and Lean reports the same situation as ``motive is not type correct''.
Without step~2, the tactic would produce a term that the kernel rejects.

\subsection{Example: $0 + n = n$ with Tactics}
\label{sec:zero-add-tactics}

In our system the proof of \S\ref{sec:zero-add} becomes the following script,
shown with the notation of this paper; the runnable version, which writes $\add\;\zero\;n$ for $0 + n$, is
\texttt{examples/zero-add.leanmini}.
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
intro n
induction n
rfl
change succ (0 + k) = succ k
rw [ih]
\end{lstlisting}
The proof state evolves as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Initially there is one goal, $\langle \cdot \vdash \hole{0} : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n} \rangle$.
  \item \texttt{intro n} assigns $\hole{0} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{n}{\Nat}{\hole{1}}$ and leaves $\langle n : \Nat \vdash \hole{1} : 0 + n = n \rangle$.
  \item \texttt{induction n} assigns
    \[
    \hole{1} \mathrel{:=} \NatRec{0}\;(\tLam{z}{\Nat}{0 + z = z})\;\hole{2}\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{0 + k = k}{\hole{3}}})\;n
    \]
    and leaves two goals: $\langle n : \Nat \vdash \hole{2} : 0 + 0 = 0 \rangle$ and $\langle n : \Nat, k : \Nat, \mathit{ih} : 0 + k = k \vdash \hole{3} : 0 + \tsucc\;k = \tsucc\;k \rangle$.
  \item \texttt{rfl} closes the first goal with $\hole{2} \mathrel{:=} \refl{1}\;\Nat\;(0 + 0)$, since $0 + 0 \conv 0$.
  \item In the second goal, $0 + k$ does not occur syntactically, so \texttt{rw [ih]} would find nothing.
    \texttt{change} first exposes it, using $0 + \tsucc\;k \conv \tsucc\;(0 + k)$: it assigns $\hole{3} \mathrel{:=} \hole{4}$ with the goal $\hole{4} : \tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;k$.
    In Lean, rewriting with the lemma \texttt{Nat.add\_succ}, which states $n + \tsucc\;m = \tsucc\;(n + m)$, produces the same goal.
  \item \texttt{rw [ih]} abstracts $0 + k$ to get $C = (\tsucc\;x = \tsucc\;k)$.
    With $T = (\tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;k)$ for the current goal, it assigns
    \[
    \hole{4} \mathrel{:=} \EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;(0 + k)\;(\tLam{x}{\Nat}{C \to T})\;(\tLam{p}{T}{p})\;k\;\mathit{ih}\;\hole{5}.
    \]
    The new goal $\hole{5} : \tsucc\;k = \tsucc\;k$ is closed at once by \texttt{rfl}, with $\hole{5} \mathrel{:=} \refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\tsucc\;k)$.
\end{enumerate}
No goals remain.
Substituting the assignments into $\hole{0}$ gives a closed term, and the kernel runs $\textsc{Check}(\cdot, t, \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n})$ on it.
The term differs from the hand-written one of \S\ref{sec:zero-add} in two places:
it starts with $\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\ldots\;n}$ because of \texttt{intro}, and its step uses the motive built by \texttt{rw}.
Both are proofs of the same proposition, and the kernel does not care which one it receives.

\subsection{Why Tactics Need Not Be Trusted}

The kernel checks the final term, so tactics do not have to be correct for the system to be sound.
A buggy tactic can fail, or it can produce an ill-typed term, which the kernel rejects; it cannot make the kernel accept a false theorem.
The checks that tactics perform themselves, such as \textsc{Check} in \texttt{exact} or the motive check in \texttt{rw}, exist only to report errors early and clearly.
The trusted part of the system is therefore small: Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer}, the reduction and comparison functions of \S\ref{sec:machinery}, and the signature of \S\ref{sec:inductive}.

Lean's tactic framework is far richer than the one sketched here.
It has metavariables solved by unification, an elaborator that fills in implicit arguments and expands notation such as \texttt{0 + n},
an \texttt{induction} that reverts dependent hypotheses, and automation such as \texttt{simp}.
All of this lives on the untrusted side: Lean's kernel, like ours, only ever sees complete terms~\cite{moura2021lean4}.


\section{Under the Hood: Substitution, $\alpha$-Equivalence, and Conversion}
\label{sec:machinery}

The previous sections treated three operations on terms as black boxes:
substitution $\subst{B}{x}{a}$, used by \textsc{T-App}, by \textsc{Freshen}, and by every computation step;
\textsc{Whnf}, used by \textsc{Infer} to expose a $\Pi$ or a $\mathsf{Sort}$;
and \textsc{IsDefEq}, used by \textsc{Check} to decide $A \conv B$.
These operations are part of the trusted kernel, and most kernel bugs hide in them, because they must handle the names of bound variables correctly.
This section opens the boxes.
\S\ref{sec:subst} defines substitution, and \S\ref{sec:capture} shows the same naming problem in contexts.
\S\ref{sec:alpha} compares terms up to the names of bound variables.
\S\ref{sec:conversion} defines computation and definitional equality, and \S\ref{sec:iota-data}--\ref{sec:whnf} give the algorithms.

\subsection{Free Variables and Substitution}
\label{sec:subst}

$\Pi$ and $\lambda$ \emph{bind} their variable: in $\tLam{x}{A}{t}$, occurrences of $x$
inside $t$ refer to the argument. The binder's scope is the body only; $x$ is not bound
in the annotation $A$.
A variable occurrence that is not bound by an enclosing $\Pi$ or $\lambda$ is \emph{free}.

\begin{definition}[Free variables]
\begin{align*}
\FV(\Sort{u}) &= \emptyset &
\FV(\tPi{x}{A}{B}) &= \FV(A) \cup (\FV(B) \setminus \{x\}) \\
\FV(x) &= \{x\} &
\FV(\tLam{x}{A}{t}) &= \FV(A) \cup (\FV(t) \setminus \{x\}) \\
\FV(t\;s) &= \FV(t) \cup \FV(s)
\end{align*}
\end{definition}

\noindent For example, $\FV(\tLam{x}{P}{f\;x\;y}) = \{P, f, y\}$, and $\FV(\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}) = \emptyset$, so the latter is a closed term.
Constants (\S\ref{sec:constants}) are never bound, so $\FV(c) = \emptyset$.

We write $\subst{t}{x}{s}$ for the result of replacing the free occurrences
of $x$ in $t$ with $s$.
The only subtle case is a binder. Consider $\subst{(\tLam{y}{A}{x})}{x}{y}$. The body
says ``ignore the argument and return the outer $x$''. Replacing $x$ by $y$
naively gives $\tLam{y}{A}{y}$, the identity function, which means something else:
the free $y$ has been \emph{captured} by the binder. Substitution must avoid this
by renaming the binder first.

\begin{definition}[Capture-avoiding substitution]

For $\square \in \{\Pi, \lambda\}$:

\begin{align*}
\subst{x}{x}{s} &= s \\
\subst{y}{x}{s} &= y && (y \neq x) \\
\subst{\Sort{u}}{x}{s} &= \Sort{u} \\
\subst{(t_1\;t_2)}{x}{s} &= \subst{t_1}{x}{s}\;\;\subst{t_2}{x}{s} \\
\subst{(\square(x{:}A).\,B)}{x}{s} &= \square(x{:}\subst{A}{x}{s}).\,B
  && \text{(we say that $x$ is shadowed)} \\
\subst{(\square(y{:}A).\,B)}{x}{s} &= \square(y{:}\subst{A}{x}{s}).\,\subst{B}{x}{s}
  && (y \neq x,\; y \notin \FV(s)) \\
\subst{(\square(y{:}A).\,B)}{x}{s} &= \square(z{:}\subst{A}{x}{s}).\,\subst{(\subst{B}{y}{z})}{x}{s}
  && (y \neq x,\; y \in \FV(s),\; z \text{ fresh})
\end{align*}

\noindent Here ``$z$ fresh'' means $z \notin \FV(s) \cup \FV(B) \cup \{x\}$.

\end{definition}

\noindent The following examples exercise each binder case.
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\;=\;}l@{\qquad}l}
\subst{(\tPi{h}{P}{P})}{P}{Q} & \tPi{h}{Q}{Q} & \text{no capture possible; the \textsc{T-App} step of \S\ref{sec:examples}} \\
\subst{(\tLam{x}{A}{x})}{x}{s} & \tLam{x}{A}{x} & \text{$x$ is shadowed; the body is untouched} \\
\subst{(\tLam{y}{x}{y})}{x}{s} & \tLam{y}{s}{y} & \text{the annotation is outside the scope of $y$} \\
\subst{(\tLam{y}{A}{x\;y})}{x}{f\;y} & \tLam{z}{A}{f\;y\;z} & \text{$y \in \FV(f\;y)$, so the binder is renamed to $z$}
