\end{array}
\]
In the last example, the free $y$ of the replacement still refers to the outer $y$, and the bound variable, now $z$, still refers to the argument.
Without the renaming, the result would be $\tLam{y}{A}{f\;y\;y}$, which passes its argument twice.

\subsection{Variable Capture in Contexts}
\label{sec:capture}

It is tempting to drop the side condition $x \notin \dom(\Gamma)$ of \textsc{C-Ext} and let a new assumption simply shadow an old one, as most programming languages do.
Doing so makes the kernel unsound.
Consider
\[
t = \tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{y}{x}{\tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{y}}}.
\]
The variable $y$ has the \emph{outer} $x$ as its type, and the innermost $\lambda$ ignores its argument.
So the correct type of $t$ is
\[
\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{y}{x}{\tPi{x'}{\Sort{0}}{x}}}.
\]
A checker without \textsc{Freshen} looks up $y$ in the context $x : \Sort{0}, y : x, x : \Sort{0}$ and returns its type, the bare name $x$.
At that point $x$ refers to the inner binder, and the checker returns
\[
\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{y}{x}{\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{x}}},
\]
which says ``from any element of any type, produce an element of every type''.
Given $A : \Sort{0}$ and $a : A$, the term $t\;A\;a$ then has type $\tPi{B}{\Sort{0}}{B}$, a proof of False.
Such $A$ and $a$ exist even in the empty context: $A = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$ is itself a proposition (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}), and the identity function $a = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}$ proves it.

With \textsc{Freshen}, the innermost binder is renamed to $x'$ before it enters the context,
so the context becomes $x : \Sort{0}, y : x, x' : \Sort{0}$, the lookup of $y$ returns $x$, which still refers to the outer binder,
and \textsc{Infer} returns the correct type above.

The problem is the same as in substitution (\S\ref{sec:subst}): a name is moved into a scope where it means something else.
It affects any representation that identifies variables by name, whether the context is a list or a hash map.
There are three common remedies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Reject shadowing outright. This is the simplest option, but the reserved name $\_$ used by $A \to B$ must be exempt and never added to the context.
  \item Rename on entry, as \textsc{Freshen} does.
  \item Represent bound variables by position (de Bruijn indices~\cite{debruijn1972nameless}) or use the \emph{locally nameless} style, in which bound variables are indices and free variables carry unique identifiers. Lean 4 takes the latter approach.
\end{enumerate}
A test suite should include $t$ above and check that the kernel either rejects it or assigns it the correct type.

\subsection{$\alpha$-Equivalence}
\label{sec:alpha}

The names of bound variables carry no meaning. For example, $\tLam{x}{A}{x}$ and $\tLam{y}{A}{y}$ are the same function, and
$\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$ and $\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{Q \to Q}$ are the same proposition. Terms that differ only in the names
of bound variables are called \emph{$\alpha$-equivalent}.
A kernel cannot compare types with plain syntactic equality, which would reject the second pair.

\begin{definition}[$\alpha$-equivalence]
\label{def:alpha}

$\alphaeq$ is the smallest congruence on terms containing, for $\square \in \{\Pi, \lambda\}$,

\[
\square(x{:}A).\,B \;\alphaeq\; \square(y{:}A).\,\subst{B}{x}{y}
\qquad \text{whenever } y \notin \FV(B).
\]

\end{definition}

This definition is easy to state but not directly executable, since it does not say which names to choose. An implementation
instead walks both terms in lockstep and remembers, for each side, the list of binders passed so far. A bound variable is
then identified by \emph{which} binder it refers to, not by its name.

To describe this walk, we use a judgment of the form $E_1; E_2 \vdash s \alphaeq t$, where $E_1$ and $E_2$ are lists of names.
The list $E_1$ records the binders that enclose $s$, from the outermost to the innermost, and $E_2$ records those that enclose $t$.
The judgment reads: ``$s$, placed inside the binders $E_1$, and $t$, placed inside the binders $E_2$, are the same term up to the names
of bound variables''. Two lists are needed because the two terms may use different names for corresponding binders.
For example, comparing $\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{B}{x}}$ with $\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}}$ passes two binders on each side and arrives at
\[
x, y;\; a, b \vdash x \alphaeq a,
\]
which holds because $x$ and $a$ both refer to the outer of the two binders. Comparing two whole terms starts from empty lists,
$\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$. The same symbol $\alphaeq$ appears in Definition~\ref{def:alpha} and in the judgment;
the prefix $E_1; E_2 \vdash$ distinguishes the judgment, and Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha} below shows that the two agree.

To say ``the same binder'' precisely, let $\mathit{idx}(E, x)$ be the position of the last occurrence of $x$ in $E$, counted from
the right starting at $0$, or undefined if $x \notin E$. In the example, $\mathit{idx}(x, y;\, x) = \mathit{idx}(a, b;\, a) = 1$.
Taking the \emph{last} occurrence handles shadowing: in $\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{x}{B}{x}}$ the body refers to the inner $x$.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\begin{mathpar}
\inferrule{\quad}{E_1; E_2 \vdash \Sort{u} \alphaeq \Sort{u}}\rulename{$\alpha$-Sort}
\and
\inferrule{\mathit{idx}(E_1, x) = \mathit{idx}(E_2, y) = i}{E_1; E_2 \vdash x \alphaeq y}\rulename{$\alpha$-Bound}
\and
\inferrule{x \notin E_1 \\ x \notin E_2}{E_1; E_2 \vdash x \alphaeq x}\rulename{$\alpha$-Free}
\and
\inferrule{E_1; E_2 \vdash A \alphaeq A' \\ E_1, x; E_2, y \vdash B \alphaeq B'}{E_1; E_2 \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} \alphaeq \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}}\rulename{$\alpha$-Pi}
\and
\inferrule{E_1; E_2 \vdash A \alphaeq A' \\ E_1, x; E_2, y \vdash t \alphaeq t'}{E_1; E_2 \vdash \tLam{x}{A}{t} \alphaeq \tLam{y}{A'}{t'}}\rulename{$\alpha$-Lam}
\and
\inferrule{E_1; E_2 \vdash t_1 \alphaeq t_1' \\ E_1; E_2 \vdash t_2 \alphaeq t_2'}{E_1; E_2 \vdash t_1\;t_2 \alphaeq t_1'\;t_2'}\rulename{$\alpha$-App}
\end{mathpar}
\caption{Algorithmic $\alpha$-equivalence. By Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha}, two terms $s$ and $t$ are $\alpha$-equivalent iff $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$.}
\label{fig:alpha}
\end{figure}

Free variables are compared by name ($\alpha$-Free), and bound variables by position ($\alpha$-Bound). A variable that is bound on
one side and free on the other is never equal to anything, which is why there is no rule for that case. Because both sides descend
through binders together, $E_1$ and $E_2$ always have the same length. So comparing positions counted from the right is the same
as comparing positions counted from the left, and an implementation may store each list as a map from names to binding depths,
provided it restores the previous entry when it leaves a binder. Using positions instead of names everywhere gives the
\emph{de Bruijn representation}~\cite{debruijn1972nameless}, in which $\alpha$-equivalent terms are syntactically identical.

Constants (\S\ref{sec:constants}) are compared by name, like free variables.

\paragraph{Examples.}
The first example of \S\ref{sec:examples} ended by comparing the inferred type with the stated one, where $P \to P$ abbreviates $\tPi{\_}{P}{P}$:
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\qquad}l}
\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}} \alphaeq \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{\_}{P}{P}} & \text{by $\alpha$-Pi, needs} \\
\quad \cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \Sort{0} \alphaeq \Sort{0} & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Sort} \\
\quad P; P \vdash \tPi{h}{P}{P} \alphaeq \tPi{\_}{P}{P} & \text{by $\alpha$-Pi, needs} \\
\quad\quad P; P \vdash P \alphaeq P & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Bound (index $0$)} \\
\quad\quad P, h; P, \_ \vdash P \alphaeq P & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Bound (index $1$)}
\end{array}
\]
The names $h$ and $\_$ differ, but neither is ever looked up, so they do not matter.
The wrong proof of \S\ref{sec:examples} fails at the last step instead:
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\qquad}l}
\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}}} \alphaeq \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{\_}{P}{P}} & \text{by $\alpha$-Pi, needs} \\
\quad \cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \Sort{0} \alphaeq \Sort{0} & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Sort} \\
\quad P; P \vdash \tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}} \alphaeq \tPi{\_}{P}{P} & \text{by $\alpha$-Pi, needs} \\
\quad\quad P; P \vdash P \alphaeq P & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Bound (index $0$)} \\
\quad\quad P, h; P, \_ \vdash \Sort{0} \alphaeq P & \text{no rule applies}
\end{array}
\]
Positions also tell apart terms that a careless comparison of names would confuse.
$\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{A}{x}}$ and $\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{A}{b}}$ are not $\alpha$-equivalent:
the bodies reach $x, y;\, a, b \vdash x \alphaeq b$, and $\mathit{idx}$ gives $1$ for $x$ but $0$ for $b$.
Conversely, $\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{x}{A}{x}}$ and $\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{A}{b}}$ are $\alpha$-equivalent,
because the last occurrence of $x$ in $x, x$ has index $0$, the same as $b$ in $a, b$.

The rules of Fig.~\ref{fig:alpha} are a different definition from Definition~\ref{def:alpha}, so we must check that they agree.

\begin{theorem}[Correctness of algorithmic $\alpha$-equivalence]
\label{thm:alpha}
For all terms $s$ and $t$, $s \alphaeq t$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:alpha} if and only if $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$ is derivable by the rules of Fig.~\ref{fig:alpha}.
\end{theorem}

\noindent The idea of the proof is that both sides say the same thing: $s$ and $t$ have the same de Bruijn representation.
For the algorithm this is almost immediate, since its rules compare positions exactly as de Bruijn indices do.
For Definition~\ref{def:alpha}, the key fact is that renaming a bound variable does not change the de Bruijn representation.
Appendix~\ref{app:alpha} gives the full proof.

\subsection{Reduction and Conversion}
\label{sec:conversion}

Applying a $\lambda$-abstraction to an argument is computed by substituting the argument for the bound variable:
\[
(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s \;\betared\; \subst{t}{x}{s}.
\]
This step is called \emph{$\beta$-reduction}, and a subterm of the form $(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s$ is called a \emph{$\beta$-redex}.
\S\ref{sec:inductive} added two more kinds of steps: $\delta$-reduction, which unfolds a definition (\S\ref{sec:constants}),
and $\iota$-reduction, which runs a recursor on a constructor (Fig.~\ref{fig:nat} and \S\ref{sec:inductive-decl}).
We allow each step anywhere inside a term, and write $\to$ for a single step of any kind.
A term in which no step applies is in \emph{normal form}.
For example, with $\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$,
\[
\tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{(\tLam{y}{P}{y})\;h} \;\betared\; \tLam{h}{P}{(\tLam{y}{P}{y})\;h} \;\betared\; \tLam{h}{P}{h},
\]
and the last term is in normal form.
Reducing the inner redex first leads to the same result.

\emph{Definitional equality} (or \emph{conversion}) identifies terms that compute to the same result, up to the names of bound variables.

\begin{definition}[Conversion]
$s \conv t$ is the smallest equivalence relation that contains $\alphaeq$ and $\to$ and is closed under all term constructors.
\end{definition}

To decide $s \conv t$, the kernel normalizes both terms and compares the results with $\alphaeq$.
This procedure relies on two facts.
First, reduction is confluent: different reduction orders cannot lead to different normal forms, so $s \conv t$ holds exactly when the normal forms of $s$ and $t$ are $\alpha$-equivalent.
Second, every well-typed term \emph{has} a normal form, so normalization terminates.
The second fact holds for our system, but it is a deep theorem (strong normalization, \S\ref{sec:properties})~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}.
A practical kernel also caps the number of reduction steps, so that a bug cannot make it loop forever; our implementation stops after $20{,}000$ steps.

\subsection{Computation Rules as Data}
\label{sec:iota-data}

Figs.~\ref{fig:nat} and~\ref{fig:eq} write each $\iota$-rule as a separate equation, which suggests that every new inductive type needs new reduction code in the kernel.
It does not.
A kernel stores the $\iota$-rules as data in the signature, next to the recursor, and a single piece of code applies them for every inductive type.

Each recursor entry records the position of its \emph{major premise}, the argument whose constructor decides which rule applies,
and a list of \emph{rules}, one per constructor.
A rule names the constructor, the number of its \emph{fields} (the arguments that the constructor stores, as opposed to the type parameters it merely carries),
and a right-hand side $\mathit{rhs}$, an ordinary term.
Each constructor entry records how many leading arguments are parameters.
For three of our recursors, the data is as follows; type annotations on $\lambda$ are omitted.
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llllll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Recursor} & \textbf{Major} & \textbf{Constructor} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Fields} & $\mathit{rhs}$ \\
\midrule
$\NatRec{u}$ & 4th & $\zero$ & 0 & 0 & $\lambda M\,z\,s.\; z$ \\
& & $\tsucc$ & 0 & 1 & $\lambda M\,z\,s\,n.\; s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n)$ \\
$\EqRecDep{u,v}$ & 6th & $\refl{u}$ & 2 & 0 & $\lambda A\,a\,M\,m\,b.\; m$ \\
$\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v$ & 5th & $\mathsf{leaf}$ & 0 & 0 & $\lambda M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3.\; m_1$ \\
& & $\mathsf{node}$ & 0 & 1 & $\lambda M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3\,t.\; m_2\;t\;(\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;m_3\;t)$ \\
& & $\mathsf{branch}$ & 0 & 2 & $\lambda M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3\,l\,r.\; m_3\;l\;r\;(\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;m_3\;l)\;(\cdots\;r)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The $\mathit{rhs}$ takes the arguments before the major premise, then the fields of the constructor.
For example, $\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;(\tsucc\;n)$ selects the second rule and becomes
\[
(\lambda M\,z\,s\,n.\; s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n))\;M\;z\;s\;n,
\]
which $\beta$-reduces to the right-hand side of the second equation in Fig.~\ref{fig:nat}.
Likewise, the only rule of $\EqRecDep{u,v}$ fires on the term $\EqRecDep{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A'\;c)$.
The constructor $\refl{u}$ has two parameters, $A'$ and $c$, and no fields,
so the $\mathit{rhs}$ receives just $A\;a\;M\;m\;b$ and returns $m$.

\subsection{Weak Head Normal Form and Normalization}
\label{sec:whnf}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf} defines the three functions that Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} left open.
Both \textsc{Whnf} and \textsc{Normalize} view a term as a \emph{spine} $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$: a head $h$ that is not an application, applied to $n \ge 0$ arguments.
Since application associates to the left (\S\ref{sec:syntax}), $f\;a\;b\;c$ is the nested term $((f\;a)\;b)\;c$;
following the function side of each application down to $f$ gives the head, and the arguments met on the way, read from the inside out, are $a, b, c$.
Every term has exactly one such decomposition; a term that is not an application is a spine with $n = 0$.

\begin{algorithm}[ht]
\footnotesize
\caption{Weak head normalization with $\beta$, $\delta$, and $\iota$; full normalization; and definitional equality.}
\label{alg:whnf}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Function{Whnf}{$t$}
  \Loop
    \State write $t$ as a spine $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$
    \If{$h = \tLam{x}{A}{b}$ and $n \ge 1$} \Comment{$\beta$}
      \State $t \gets (\subst{b}{x}{a_1})\;a_2 \cdots a_n$
    \ElsIf{$h = c$ and $(c : C \mathrel{:=} d) \in \Sigma$} \Comment{$\delta$}
      \State $t \gets d\;a_1 \cdots a_n$
    \ElsIf{$h = c$ is a recursor with major position $p \le n$} \Comment{$\iota$}
      \State $k\;b_1 \cdots b_j \gets \Call{Whnf}{a_p}$
      \If{$k$ is a constructor with a rule $r$ of $c$, and $k$ has $q$ parameters}
        \State $t \gets r.\mathit{rhs}\;a_1 \cdots a_{p-1}\;b_{q+1} \cdots b_j\;a_{p+1} \cdots a_n$
      \Else\ \Return $t$ \Comment{stuck, e.g.\ on a variable}
      \EndIf
    \Else\ \Return $t$
    \EndIf
  \EndLoop
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Normalize}{$t$}
  \State $t \gets \Call{Whnf}{t}$
  \If{$t = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$} \Return $\tPi{x}{\Call{Normalize}{A}}{\Call{Normalize}{B}}$
  \ElsIf{$t = \tLam{x}{A}{b}$} \Return $\tLam{x}{\Call{Normalize}{A}}{\Call{Normalize}{b}}$
  \Else\ write $t$ as a spine $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$ and \Return $h\;\Call{Normalize}{a_1} \cdots \Call{Normalize}{a_n}$
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{IsDefEq}{$s, t$}
  \State \Return $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \Call{Normalize}{s} \alphaeq \Call{Normalize}{t}$ \Comment{Fig.~\ref{fig:alpha}}
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\textsc{Whnf} reduces only at the head of a term, until no rule applies there; the result is the \emph{weak head normal form}.
It never looks inside a $\lambda$, a $\Pi$, or the arguments of a stuck head.
This is enough when a caller only needs the outermost shape of a type, such as a $\Pi$ in the application case of \textsc{Infer}, and it is cheaper than full normalization.
\textsc{Normalize} first computes the weak head normal form and then normalizes every immediate subterm.
For example, with $t = \tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{h}$ and $\mathit{Id}$ as above,
\[
\textsc{Whnf}(t) = t, \qquad \textsc{Normalize}(t) = \tLam{h}{P}{h},
\]
because the head of $t$ is a $\lambda$ with no arguments, while \textsc{Normalize} continues into the annotation $\mathit{Id}\;P$.
Likewise, $\textsc{Whnf}(\mathit{Id}\;(\mathit{Id}\;P \to P)) = \mathit{Id}\;P \to P$, which already shows a $\Pi$ although its domain is not yet normal.

The three cases of \textsc{Whnf} have the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
  \item The $\iota$ case contains no reference to $\Nat$, $\Eq{}$, or $\mathsf{Tree}$. It reads the major position and the rules from the signature (\S\ref{sec:iota-data}).
    It is written once; after that, each new inductive type adds rows of data, not code.
  \item The major premise is put in weak head normal form before the rules are consulted, because it may become a constructor only after computation.
    For $2 + 1$ in \S\ref{sec:nat}, the major premise is the numeral $1 = \tsucc\;\zero$, already a constructor;
    for $\mathit{double}\;(1 + 1)$, it is $1 + 1$, which \textsc{Whnf} turns into $\tsucc\;(1 + 0)$ first.
  \item If the major premise does not become a constructor, for instance because it is a variable, the term is stuck and stays as it is; this is why $0 + n$ does not reduce (\S\ref{sec:eq}).
\end{itemize}
\textsc{IsDefEq} normalizes fully for simplicity, and our implementation does the same.
Practical kernels compare lazily instead: they reduce both sides to weak head normal form, compare the heads, and recurse into the arguments only when needed,
which avoids normalizing large terms that differ at the head.
Termination of all three functions for well-typed terms is strong normalization.

\section{Universes: Why $\mathsf{Sort}\;u$?}
\label{sec:universes}

\S\ref{sec:logic} showed that the typing rules implement a logic, and that the system is acceptable only if it is consistent.
This section asks what the type of $\Sort{0}$ should be.
It shows that the simplest choice of universes, a single universe that contains itself, makes the system inconsistent (\S\ref{sec:typetype}),
and that the hierarchy $\Sort{0} : \Sort{1} : \cdots$ with an impredicative bottom universe, as in Lean, avoids the problem (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).

\subsection{What Is the Type of $\Sort{0}$?}

A proposition variable appears in the type theory as an assumption $P : \Sort{0}$.
It can occur in two places: in a context, as in the left judgment below, or bound by $\lambda$ or $\Pi$, as in the right one:
\[
P : \Sort{0} \vdash \tLam{h}{P}{h} : P \to P
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
\vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}.
\]
The left judgment proves $P \to P$ for one fixed $P$ supplied from outside.
The right one is a single closed term that proves it for every $P$, and it can be applied later to any particular proposition;
this is what the $\forall$ rows of Fig.~\ref{fig:logic} need.

Both forms require $\Sort{0}$ to be a type.
\textsc{C-Ext}, which adds $P : \Sort{0}$ to a context, and \textsc{T-Lam} and \textsc{T-Pi}, which bind $P : \Sort{0}$, all have the premise $\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}$ for the type $A$ of the new variable.
With $A = \Sort{0}$, this premise reads $\Gamma \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{u}$ for some $u$: the universe of propositions must itself have a type.
\S\ref{sec:typetype} shows that the simplest answer, that $\Sort{0}$ is its own type, makes the system inconsistent.
\S\ref{sec:hierarchy} then presents Lean's answer, a hierarchy of universes.

\subsection{Type Is Not a Type}
\label{sec:typetype}

Suppose we replace all universes by a single universe $\mathsf{Type}$ that contains itself:
\[
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}}
\qquad
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathsf{Type} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathsf{Type}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \mathsf{Type}}
\]
Translate $\forall P.\,\varphi$ as $\tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{\varphi^\ast}$.
Then $P$ ranges over a collection that contains $\mathsf{Type}$ itself and every type built from it.
Such a collection is the type-theoretic analogue of the set of all sets, and naive set theory shows that such collections lead to contradictions.
The best-known example is \emph{Russell's paradox}:
for $R = \{\, x \mid x \notin x \,\}$, both $R \in R$ and $R \notin R$ lead to a contradiction.
Type theory has no membership test like $x \notin x$, so Russell's argument does not carry over word for word.
Girard instead adapted a related paradox about the collection of all well-orderings, due to Burali-Forti~\cite{girard1972interpretation},
and Hurkens simplified the resulting term~\cite{hurkens1995simplification}.
The result is a closed term $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ with
\[
\vdash t_{\mathrm{H}} : \tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{P},
\]
so the system is inconsistent: $\bot$ has no proof, yet $\bot^\ast$ has a term, and a kernel built on these rules accepts a proof of every statement.
The essential ingredient is a type $U$ that quantifies over all of $\mathsf{Type}$ while being a member of $\mathsf{Type}$,
which lets $U$ contain a copy of its own double power set, something no set can do.
Appendix~\ref{app:hurkens} gives $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ in full and explains how it works.


The damage reaches the algorithm as well.
Subject reduction still holds, so if $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ had a normal form, it would be a normal closed term of type $\tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p}$.
The part of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:consistency} (Appendix~\ref{app:consistency}) that analyses normal terms does not use strong normalization and carries over to $\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}$; it shows that no such normal term exists.
Hence $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ has no normal form, strong normalization fails, and \textsc{Normalize} (Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf}) runs forever on it.

\subsection{A Hierarchy with an Impredicative Bottom}
\label{sec:hierarchy}

The second answer is that $\Sort{0}$ lives in a larger universe, which lives in a larger one still:
\[
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}}\rulename{T-Sort}
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\Sort{0} : \Sort{1} : \Sort{2} : \cdots.
\]
No universe contains itself.
A $\Pi$ type takes an argument from one universe and returns a type in another, so \textsc{T-Pi} must also say which universe the $\Pi$ type itself belongs to.
Lean's answer uses the function $\imax$:
\[
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \Sort{v}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \Sort{\imax(u, v)}}\rulename{T-Pi}
\qquad
\imax(u, v) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } v = 0, \\
\max(u, v) & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
The case split in $\imax$ makes a $\Pi$ type impredicative when its body is a proposition, and predicative otherwise.

\paragraph{Propositions are impredicative.}
If the body $B$ is a proposition ($v = 0$), the whole $\Pi$ is a proposition, whatever it quantifies over.
In particular $(\forall P.\,\varphi)^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}$ is in $\Sort{0}$, although it quantifies over all of $\Sort{0}$.
A universe that contains types quantifying over itself is called \emph{impredicative}.
Because every translated formula lies in $\Sort{0}$, the premise $\psi^\ast : \Sort{0}$ of $\forall$-elim always holds,
so a universal statement can be instantiated with any proposition, even with itself.
For example, with $\mathit{id} = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}$,
\[
\mathit{id} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} : \Sort{0},
\]
so $\mathit{id}\;(\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P})\;\mathit{id}$ is well typed, with type $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$.
The same case makes $\forall n : \mathsf{Nat},\, n + 0 = n$ a proposition, even though $\mathsf{Nat}$ lives in $\Sort{1}$; \S\ref{sec:nat} relies on this for induction.

\paragraph{Types are predicative.}
If the body is not a proposition ($v \ge 1$), the $\Pi$ lives in the larger of the two universes.
A type that quantifies over $\Sort{u}$ then lives in $\Sort{(\max(u+1, v))}$, which is never $\Sort{u}$:
\[
\inferrule*[right=T-Pi]
  {\inferrule*[right=T-Sort]{ }{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}} \\ \Gamma, x : \Sort{u} \vdash B : \Sort{v}}
  {\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{\Sort{u}}{B} : \Sort{(\max(u+1, v))}}
\]
This property is called \emph{predicativity}.
For example, the identity on types $\tLam{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tLam{a}{A}{a}}$ has type $\tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{A \to A}$, which lives in $\Sort{2}$,
so it cannot be applied to its own type; a copy at $\Sort{2}$ can.
Each level holds the level beneath it, and in practice a few levels suffice; higher levels appear when one quantifies over large collections, such as the category of all small categories.

\paragraph{Why this is safe.}
Impredicativity looks like the self-reference that \S\ref{sec:typetype} warned against, but it is confined:
$\Sort{0}$ contains types that quantify over $\Sort{0}$, yet $\Sort{0}$ is not a member of itself.
Coquand showed that one impredicative universe at the bottom is consistent~\cite{coquand1988calculus},
whereas Girard's paradox can already be derived once two levels are impredicative~\cite{hurkens1995simplification}.
With these rules the system is consistent and strongly normalizing (\S\ref{sec:properties}).

\subsection{Comparison with Lean}

In Lean~\cite{moura2021lean4}, $\Sort{0}$ is $\mathsf{Prop}$, $\Sort{(u+1)}$ is $\mathsf{Type}\;u$, and $\Pi$ types are assigned universes with $\imax$ exactly as above.
Two differences remain.
First, $\mathsf{Prop}$ in Lean has \emph{definitional proof irrelevance}: any two proofs of the same proposition are definitionally equal.
Our conversion does not identify proofs; adding this would make conversion depend on types, so the simple ``normalize and compare'' check of \S\ref{sec:conversion} would no longer suffice.
Second, Lean has \emph{universe polymorphism}, so definitions can be stated once for all levels $u$, and $\imax$ then matters for level variables as well.
In our system every level is a concrete number.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Design choices for universes.}
\label{tab:universes}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Design} & \textbf{Quantifies over} & \textbf{Drawback} \\
\midrule
No universes & values only & cannot say ``for every proposition'' \\
$\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}$ & everything & inconsistent \\
Two sorts $\ast : \square$ & $\ast$ only & $\square$ itself has no type \\
$\Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}$ with $\max$ & any level & $\forall$ over propositions is not a proposition \\
$\Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}$ with $\imax$ (Lean) & any level & normalization is harder to prove \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\section{Properties}
\label{sec:properties}

We state, without proof, the standard properties of the core system of \S\S\ref{sec:syntax}--\ref{sec:examples}, with the universes of \S\ref{sec:universes} and without the constants of \S\ref{sec:inductive}.
It is a Pure Type System: the Calculus of Constructions~\cite{coquand1988calculus} with a hierarchy of predicative universes above its impredicative $\Sort{0}$,
close to Luo's Extended Calculus of Constructions~\cite{luo1990extended}.
The first three properties below hold for every functional Pure Type System~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}.
Strong normalization is much harder in the presence of impredicativity and needs Girard's method of reducibility candidates~\cite{girard1972interpretation,coquand1988calculus,luo1990extended}.
The end of this section revisits them for inductive types.

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of types]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ and $\Gamma \vdash t : B$, then $A \conv B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Type correctness]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$, then either $A = \Sort{u}$ for some $u$, or $\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}$ for some $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Subject reduction]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ and $t \betared t'$, then $\Gamma \vdash t' : A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Strong normalization]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$, then every sequence of $\beta$-reductions starting from $t$ is finite.
\end{theorem}

Together these give the two guarantees we want from a kernel.
\emph{Decidability}: Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} terminates on every input, so whether a proof is correct can always be determined.
\emph{Consistency}: no closed term proves False.

\begin{theorem}[Consistency]
\label{thm:consistency}
There is no closed term $t$ with $\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$.
\end{theorem}

\noindent By strong normalization and subject reduction, such a term would have a normal form of the same type.
A closed normal term whose type is a $\Pi$ must be a $\lambda$:
it cannot be a variable or start with one, since no variable is in scope, and universes and $\Pi$ types have a universe as their type.
So the normal form is $\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{s}$ with $P : \Sort{0} \vdash s : P$ and $s$ normal.
A normal term is a universe, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or a variable applied to arguments, and none of these can have type $P$ in that context:
the only variable available is $P$ itself, whose type is $\Sort{0}$, not $P$.
Appendix~\ref{app:consistency} gives the full proof, including the facts about typing and conversion that this argument uses.

\paragraph{With inductive types.}
The $\iota$-rules of \S\ref{sec:inductive} do not overlap with each other or with $\beta$, so reduction remains confluent.
Subject reduction, strong normalization, and consistency are known for the Calculus of Inductive Constructions~\cite{werner1994theorie}, of which our system is a small fragment.
The short consistency argument above no longer suffices by itself, because normal forms now include stuck recursor applications;
consistency follows from strong normalization by a more careful analysis of normal forms.
Lean's full theory, with definitional proof irrelevance and general inductive types, has subtler metatheory~\cite{carneiro2019type}.

\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pat}}
\label{app:pat}

\paragraph{The precise statement.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:pat} leaves implicit which proposition variables are in scope.
For the proof we make them explicit and write $\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi$, where $\Theta$ is a list of distinct proposition variables
and every proposition variable free in $\Delta$ or $\varphi$ belongs to $\Theta$.
The rules of Fig.~\ref{fig:logic} then read
\begin{mathpar}
\inferrule{\varphi \in \Delta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta; \Delta, \varphi \vdash \psi}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi \\ \Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \psi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta, P; \Delta \vdash \varphi \\ P \notin \Theta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi \\ \FV(\psi) \subseteq \Theta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi}}
\end{mathpar}
The side condition $P \notin \FV(\Delta)$ of Fig.~\ref{fig:logic} is now implied by $P \notin \Theta$.
Formulas are taken up to $\alpha$-equivalence, and $\varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast$ stands for $\tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}$ with $x$ fresh.

The context $\Delta^\ast$ of \S\ref{sec:logic} lists the proposition variables first and the hypotheses after them.
The proof has to extend contexts on the right, so it is convenient to allow any order.

\begin{definition}[Representation]
A context $\Gamma$ \emph{represents} $(\Theta; \Delta)$ if $\ctxok{\Gamma}$ and $\Gamma$ consists of
one assumption $P : \Sort{0}$ for each $P \in \Theta$ and one assumption $h : \chi^\ast$ for each $\chi \in \Delta$, in some order.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem~\ref{thm:pat}, precise form]
\label{thm:pat-precise}
If $\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi$ and $\Gamma$ represents $(\Theta; \Delta)$, then $\Gamma \vdash t : \varphi^\ast$ for some term $t$.
\end{theorem}

\noindent The context $\Delta^\ast$ represents $(\Theta; \Delta)$ when $\Theta$ lists the free proposition variables;
it is well formed by Lemma~\ref{lem:formula-type} below and \textsc{C-Ext}.
So Theorem~\ref{thm:pat} is the special case $\Gamma = \Delta^\ast$.

\paragraph{Facts about the translation.}
Translation commutes with substitution: $(\subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi})^\ast = \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast}$.
This is a routine induction on $\varphi$.

\begin{lemma}[Formulas are propositions]
\label{lem:formula-type}
If $\ctxok{\Gamma}$ and $(P : \Sort{0}) \in \Gamma$ for every $P \in \FV(\varphi)$, then $\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $\varphi$.
For $P$, use \textsc{T-Var}.
For $\varphi \to \psi$, the induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}$,
so $\Gamma, x : \varphi^\ast$ is well formed by \textsc{C-Ext} for a fresh $x$.
The induction hypothesis for $\psi$ in that context gives $\Sort{0}$, and \textsc{T-Pi} gives $\Sort{\imax(0, 0)} = \Sort{0}$.
For $\forall Q.\,\chi$, rename $Q$ so that $Q \notin \dom(\Gamma)$.
\textsc{T-Sort} gives $\Gamma \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{1}$, so $\Gamma, Q : \Sort{0}$ is well formed,
and \textsc{T-Pi} with the induction hypothesis for $\chi$ gives $\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}$.
\end{proof}

\noindent The last case is where impredicativity is used. With $\max$ in place of $\imax$, $(\forall Q.\,\chi)^\ast$ would live in $\Sort{1}$,
and the $\forall$-elim case below would hold only for formulas $\psi$ without $\forall$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pat-precise}]
By induction on the derivation of $\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi$, for all $\Gamma$ at once.
Each case builds the typing derivation shown in the right column of Fig.~\ref{fig:logic}.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Hypothesis.} $\Gamma$ contains $h : \varphi^\ast$, so $\Gamma \vdash h : \varphi^\ast$ by \textsc{T-Var}.
  \item \emph{$\to$-intro.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:formula-type}, $\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}$.
    For a fresh $h$, the context $\Gamma, h : \varphi^\ast$ is well formed and represents $(\Theta; \Delta, \varphi)$.
    The induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma, h : \varphi^\ast \vdash t : \psi^\ast$,
    and \textsc{T-Lam} gives $\Gamma \vdash \tLam{h}{\varphi^\ast}{t} : \tPi{h}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}$.
    This type is $\varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast$, since the free variables of $\psi^\ast$ are proposition variables and $h$ is not one of them.
  \item \emph{$\to$-elim.} The induction hypotheses give $\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}$ with $x \notin \FV(\psi^\ast)$ and $\Gamma \vdash a : \varphi^\ast$.
    \textsc{T-App} gives $\Gamma \vdash f\;a : \subst{\psi^\ast}{x}{a} = \psi^\ast$.
  \item \emph{$\forall$-intro.} Renaming $P$ if necessary, assume $P \notin \dom(\Gamma)$;
    a routine induction shows that renaming a variable of $\Theta$ to a fresh one preserves derivations.
    By \textsc{T-Sort} and \textsc{C-Ext}, $\Gamma, P : \Sort{0}$ is well formed, and it represents $(\Theta, P; \Delta)$.
    The induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma, P : \Sort{0} \vdash t : \varphi^\ast$,
    and \textsc{T-Lam} gives $\Gamma \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{t} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}$.
  \item \emph{$\forall$-elim.} The induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}$,
    and Lemma~\ref{lem:formula-type} gives $\Gamma \vdash \psi^\ast : \Sort{0}$.
    \textsc{T-App} gives $\Gamma \vdash f\;\psi^\ast : \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast} = (\subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi})^\ast$. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha}}
\label{app:alpha}

Both sides of Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha} turn out to say the same thing: $s$ and $t$ have the same de Bruijn representation.
We first define that representation, and then relate it to the algorithm (Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-alg}) and to the definition (Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-def}).

\paragraph{Nameless terms.}
A \emph{nameless term} is built like a term, except that binders carry no names and a bound variable is written as a number $\#i$:
\[
d ::= \Sort{u} \mid \#i \mid x \mid \Pi\,d.\,d \mid \lambda\,d.\,d \mid d\;d
\]
Free variables keep their names.
For a list of names $E$, the nameless form $\db{t}{E}$ of a term $t$ that occurs under the binders $E$ is
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}l@{\qquad}r@{\;}l}
\db{\Sort{u}}{E} &= \Sort{u} &
\db{x}{E} &= \begin{cases} \#\mathit{idx}(E, x) & \text{if } x \in E, \\ x & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \\[10pt]
\db{\tPi{x}{A}{B}}{E} &= \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{B}{E, x} &
\db{\tLam{x}{A}{t}}{E} &= \lambda\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{t}{E, x} \\[4pt]
\db{t_1\;t_2}{E} &= \db{t_1}{E}\;\db{t_2}{E}.
\end{array}
\]
Equality of nameless terms is plain syntactic equality.
Note that $\db{t}{E}$ has the same outermost shape as $t$, except that a variable may become either a number or a name.
Constants (\S\ref{sec:constants}) are left unchanged, like universes, and are compared by name; they add only trivial cases below.

\begin{lemma}[The algorithm compares nameless forms]
\label{lem:alpha-alg}
For all $E_1$, $E_2$, $s$, and $t$: $E_1; E_2 \vdash s \alphaeq t$ is derivable if and only if $\db{s}{E_1} = \db{t}{E_2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $s$, for all $t$, $E_1$, and $E_2$.
For each shape of $s$, exactly one rule of Fig.~\ref{fig:alpha} can conclude the judgment, and its premises match the equations for $\db{\cdot}{}$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $s = \Sort{u}$, both sides hold exactly when $t = \Sort{u}$, by $\alpha$-Sort.
  \item If $s = x$, the nameless forms can be equal only if $t$ is a variable $y$.
    If $x \in E_1$, then $\db{x}{E_1} = \#\mathit{idx}(E_1, x)$, and equality holds exactly when $y \in E_2$ and $\mathit{idx}(E_2, y) = \mathit{idx}(E_1, x)$, which is the premise of $\alpha$-Bound.
    If $x \notin E_1$, then $\db{x}{E_1} = x$, and equality holds exactly when $y \notin E_2$ and $y = x$, which is the premise of $\alpha$-Free.
    A number never equals a name, matching the absence of a rule for a variable that is bound on one side only.
  \item If $s = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$, equality holds exactly when $t = \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}$ with $\db{A}{E_1} = \db{A'}{E_2}$ and $\db{B}{E_1, x} = \db{B'}{E_2, y}$.
    By the induction hypothesis, these are the premises of $\alpha$-Pi.
    The cases $\lambda$ and application are the same. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

The definition of $\alphaeq$ involves substitution, so we need two facts about how nameless forms behave under renaming.
The first says that $\db{t}{E}$ depends on $E$ only through the free variables of $t$.

\begin{lemma}[Agreement]
\label{lem:alpha-agree}
If $\mathit{idx}(E_1, v) = \mathit{idx}(E_2, v)$ for every $v \in \FV(t)$, with both sides possibly undefined, then $\db{t}{E_1} = \db{t}{E_2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $t$, for all $E_1$ and $E_2$.
The variable case is the assumption.
Under a binder $x$, the lists $E_1, x$ and $E_2, x$ again agree on the free variables of the body:
$x$ has position $0$ in both, and any other free variable has its position increased by one in both, or stays undefined in both.
\end{proof}

The second says that renaming a binder does not change the nameless form.
We use that substituting a variable for a variable preserves the size of a term, even when binders are renamed; this is a routine induction.

\begin{lemma}[Renaming]
\label{lem:alpha-rename}
Let $y \neq x$, $y \notin \FV(B)$, and $x, y \notin E'$.
Then $\db{B}{E, x, E'} = \db{\subst{B}{x}{y}}{E, y, E'}$ for every list $E$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on the size of $B$, for all $E$ and $E'$.
Write $L_x = E, x, E'$ and $L_y = E, y, E'$; they differ only in one entry, at the same position.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $B = x$, then $\subst{B}{x}{y} = y$. Since $x, y \notin E'$, both $\mathit{idx}(L_x, x)$ and $\mathit{idx}(L_y, y)$ equal the length of $E'$.
  \item If $B = v \neq x$, then $v \neq y$ because $y \notin \FV(B)$, and $\subst{B}{x}{y} = v$.
    The position of $v$ is the same in $L_x$ and $L_y$, or undefined in both.
  \item Universes and applications are immediate from the definitions and the induction hypothesis.
  \item Let $B = \tPi{w}{C}{D}$; the case of $\lambda$ is the same.
    The annotation $C$ is handled by the induction hypothesis in each case below, so we consider only the body.
    There are three cases, following the definition of substitution.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item \emph{$w = x$.} Then $\subst{B}{x}{y} = \tPi{x}{\subst{C}{x}{y}}{D}$, and we need $\db{D}{L_x, x} = \db{D}{L_y, x}$.
        We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-agree}.
        The variable $x$ has position $0$ in both lists.
        Any other $v \in \FV(D)$ differs from $y$, since $y \notin \FV(B)$, so its position is the same in both lists, or undefined in both.
      \item \emph{$w \notin \{x, y\}$.} Then $\subst{B}{x}{y} = \tPi{w}{\subst{C}{x}{y}}{\subst{D}{x}{y}}$.
        The induction hypothesis for $D$, with $E'$ extended by $w$, gives $\db{D}{L_x, w} = \db{\subst{D}{x}{y}}{L_y, w}$.
      \item \emph{$w = y$.} The binder would capture $y$, so substitution renames it to a fresh $z \notin \FV(D) \cup \{x, y\}$:
        $\subst{B}{x}{y} = \tPi{z}{\subst{C}{x}{y}}{\subst{(\subst{D}{y}{z})}{x}{y}}$.
        The induction hypothesis for $D$, renaming its last binder $y$ to $z$, gives $\db{D}{L_x, y} = \db{\subst{D}{y}{z}}{L_x, z}$.
        The induction hypothesis for $\subst{D}{y}{z}$, which has the size of $D$ and no free $y$, with $E'$ extended by $z$,
        gives $\db{\subst{D}{y}{z}}{L_x, z} = \db{\subst{(\subst{D}{y}{z})}{x}{y}}{L_y, z}$. \qedhere
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The definition compares nameless forms]
\label{lem:alpha-def}
If $s \alphaeq t$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:alpha}, then $\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}$ for every $E$.
Conversely, if $\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}$ for some $E$, then $s \alphaeq t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the first part, let $s \sim t$ mean that $\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}$ for every $E$.
This relation is an equivalence, and it is a congruence, because $\db{\cdot}{}$ is defined constructor by constructor.
It contains the defining equation of Definition~\ref{def:alpha}:
if $y \notin \FV(B)$, then $\db{\tPi{x}{A}{B}}{E} = \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{B}{E, x}$ and $\db{\tPi{y}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{y}}}{E} = \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{\subst{B}{x}{y}}{E, y}$,
and the bodies are equal by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-rename} with $E'$ empty (the case $y = x$ is trivial).
Since $\alphaeq$ is the smallest congruence containing that equation, $s \alphaeq t$ implies $s \sim t$.

For the converse, we use induction on the size of $s$, for all $t$ and $E$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $s$ is a variable, so is $t$.
    If both nameless forms are $\#i$, both variables are the entry at position $i$ of $E$, so $s = t$.
    If both are names, then $s = t$ directly.
  \item Universes and applications follow from the induction hypothesis and the congruence of $\alphaeq$.
  \item Let $s = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$, so that $t = \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}$ with $\db{A}{E} = \db{A'}{E}$ and $\db{B}{E, x} = \db{B'}{E, y}$.
    The induction hypothesis gives $A \alphaeq A'$.
    For the bodies, choose $z \notin \FV(B) \cup \FV(B') \cup \{x, y\}$.
    Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-rename} with $E'$ empty gives $\db{B}{E, x} = \db{\subst{B}{x}{z}}{E, z}$ and $\db{B'}{E, y} = \db{\subst{B'}{y}{z}}{E, z}$,
    so $\db{\subst{B}{x}{z}}{E, z} = \db{\subst{B'}{y}{z}}{E, z}$.
    Since $\subst{B}{x}{z}$ has the size of $B$, the induction hypothesis gives $\subst{B}{x}{z} \alphaeq \subst{B'}{y}{z}$.
    Then
    \[
    \tPi{x}{A}{B} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{z}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{z}} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{z}{A'}{\subst{B'}{y}{z}} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{y}{A'}{B'},
    \]
    by the defining equation, by congruence, and by the defining equation read backwards.
    The case of $\lambda$ is the same. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha}]
If $s \alphaeq t$, then $\db{s}{\cdot} = \db{t}{\cdot}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-def}, and $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-alg}.
Conversely, if $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$, then $\db{s}{\cdot} = \db{t}{\cdot}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-alg}, and $s \alphaeq t$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-def}.
\end{proof}

\section{Hurkens' Paradox}
\label{app:hurkens}

This appendix gives the term $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ of \S\ref{sec:typetype} in full (Fig.~\ref{fig:hurkens}) and explains how it works.
We checked it with the kernel of \texttt{chapters/01}, with \textsc{T-Sort} changed to $\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}$:
\textsc{Infer} returns exactly $\tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p}$ for $t_{\mathrm{H}}$, while the unchanged kernel rejects the term.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
\bot &=& \tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p}, \qquad \neg\varphi = \varphi \to \bot, \qquad \wp S = S \to \mathsf{Type} \\[4pt]
U &=& \tPi{X}{\mathsf{Type}}{((\wp\wp X \to X) \to \wp\wp X)} \\[4pt]
\tau &=& \tLam{t}{\wp\wp U}{\tLam{X}{\mathsf{Type}}{\tLam{f}{\wp\wp X \to X}{\tLam{p}{\wp X}{t\;(\tLam{x}{U}{p\;(f\;(x\;X\;f))})}}}} \\[4pt]
\sigma &=& \tLam{s}{U}{s\;U\;\tau} \\[4pt]
\Delta &=& \tLam{y}{U}{\neg\,(\tPi{p}{\wp U}{\sigma\;y\;p \to p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;y))})} \\[4pt]
\Omega &=& \tau\;(\tLam{p}{\wp U}{\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}}) \\[10pt]
t_{\mathrm{H}} &=& (\lambda (h_0 : \tPi{p}{\wp U}{(\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}) \to p\;\Omega}).\; \\
&& \qquad h_0\;\Delta\;(\tLam{x}{U}{\tLam{h_2}{\sigma\;x\;\Delta}{\tLam{h_3}{\tPi{p}{\wp U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;x))}}{
     h_3\;\Delta\;h_2\;(\tLam{p}{\wp U}{h_3\;(\tLam{y}{U}{p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;y))})})}}}) \\
&& \qquad\phantom{h_0\;\Delta\;}(\tLam{p}{\wp U}{h_0\;(\tLam{y}{U}{p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;y))})})) \\
&& (\tLam{p}{\wp U}{\tLam{h_1}{\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}}{h_1\;\Omega\;(\tLam{x}{U}{h_1\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;x))})}})
\end{array}
\]
\caption{Hurkens' paradox in a system with $\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}$. The first six lines are abbreviations, expanded in place; $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ has type $\bot$.}
\label{fig:hurkens}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{How the term works.}
Read $\wp S = S \to \mathsf{Type}$ as the type of predicates on $S$, that is, of ``subsets'' of $S$.
The type $U$ is built to contain a copy of its own double power set $\wp\wp U$:
$\tau : \wp\wp U \to U$ packs a family of subsets of $U$ into one element of $U$, and $\sigma : U \to \wp\wp U$ unpacks it, with
\[
\sigma\;(\tau\;t)\;p \;\conv\; t\;(\tLam{x}{U}{p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;x))})
\]
by $\beta$-reduction alone.
In set theory no set contains a copy of its power set (Cantor's theorem), let alone of its double power set.
$U$ can, because it quantifies over all of $\mathsf{Type}$ while being a member of $\mathsf{Type}$.

With $\sigma$ we can imitate an ordering on $U$.
Read $\sigma\;x\;p$ as ``$p$ holds for every element below $x$'',
call $p$ \emph{inductive} if $\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}$, and call $x$ \emph{well-founded} if every inductive $p$ holds of $x$.
The element $\Omega$ plays the role of ``the collection of all well-founded elements'', like the set of all ordinals in Burali-Forti's paradox.
The three arguments in $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ then say the following.
\begin{itemize}
  \item The last line proves that $\Omega$ is well-founded. Its type is the type of $h_0$.
  \item $h_0\;\Delta\;(\cdots)$ proves that the predicate $\Delta$, ``$y$ is not below itself'', is inductive, and applies the well-foundedness of $\Omega$ to it:
    $\Omega$ is not below itself. (Strictly, $\Delta\;y$ speaks of $\tau\;(\sigma\;y)$, which behaves like $y$.)
  \item The argument $\tLam{p}{\wp U}{h_0\;(\cdots)}$ proves, using the equation above, that $\Omega$ is below itself.
\end{itemize}
Applying the second to the third yields a term of type $\bot$.
$\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}$ is used in one place: $\sigma$ applies $s : U$ to $U$ itself, which requires $U : \mathsf{Type}$ although $U$ quantifies over $\mathsf{Type}$.
In the hierarchy of \S\ref{sec:hierarchy}, $U$ lives in a higher universe than the one it quantifies over, so this application is ill typed.

\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:consistency}}
\label{app:consistency}

The proof concerns the core system of \S\ref{sec:properties}: the rules of Fig.~\ref{fig:typing} with the universes of \S\ref{sec:universes}, without the constants of \S\ref{sec:inductive}.
It combines strong normalization with an analysis of the shapes of normal terms.

\paragraph{Facts about the type system.}
Besides subject reduction and strong normalization (\S\ref{sec:properties}), the proof uses the following standard properties of Pure Type Systems~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}.
Subject reduction extends from one step to any number of steps by induction on the number of steps.

\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:pts}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item \emph{Generation.} If $\Gamma \vdash t : T$, then, depending on the shape of $t$:
    \begin{itemize}
      \item if $t = x$, then $(x : A) \in \Gamma$ and $T \conv A$ for some $A$;
      \item if $t = \Sort{u}$, then $T \conv \Sort{(u+1)}$;
      \item if $t = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$, then $T \conv \Sort{w}$ for some $w$;
      \item if $t = \tLam{x}{A}{s}$, then $\Gamma, x : A \vdash s : B$ and $T \conv \tPi{x}{A}{B}$ for some $B$;
      \item if $t = f\;a$, then $\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{A}{B}$ and $\Gamma \vdash a : A$ for some $x$, $A$, and $B$.
    \end{itemize}
  \item \emph{Confluence.} If $s \conv t$, then $s$ and $t$ reduce to a common term. Consequently:
    $\tPi{x}{A}{B} \conv \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}$ implies $A \conv A'$ and $\subst{B}{x}{z} \conv \subst{B'}{y}{z}$ for a fresh $z$;
    and no two of a variable, a universe, and a $\Pi$ are convertible.
  \item \emph{Substitution.} If $s \conv t$, then $\subst{s}{z}{a} \conv \subst{t}{z}{a}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\noindent The consequences in (b) hold because a variable and a universe do not reduce at all, a $\Pi$ reduces only to a $\Pi$,
and two terms with a common reduct must therefore have the same outermost shape.

\paragraph{Shapes of normal terms.}
Recall from \S\ref{sec:whnf} that every term is a spine $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$ whose head $h$ is not an application.

\begin{lemma}[Normal forms]
\label{lem:normal-shape}
Let $n$ be a normal term with $\Gamma \vdash n : T$.
Then $n$ is a universe, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or a \emph{neutral} term $x\;a_1 \cdots a_k$ with $k \ge 0$ whose head $x$ is a variable in $\dom(\Gamma)$.
Moreover, if $k \ge 1$, then $\Gamma \vdash x : C$ for some $C$ that is convertible to a $\Pi$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $n = h\;a_1 \cdots a_k$.
If $k = 0$, then $n = h$ is a universe, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or a variable, and a variable is in $\dom(\Gamma)$ by generation.

Let $k \ge 1$.
Applying the generation lemma for application $k$ times, from the outside in, shows that every prefix $h\;a_1 \cdots a_i$ is typable,
and in particular $\Gamma \vdash h : \tPi{y}{A}{B}$ for some $y$, $A$, and $B$, from the innermost application $h\;a_1$.
The head $h$ is not a $\lambda$, since $h\;a_1$ would then be a $\beta$-redex inside the normal term $n$.
It is not a universe or a $\Pi$ either: by generation, its type would be convertible to a universe, and by confluence a universe is not convertible to $\tPi{y}{A}{B}$.
So $h$ is a variable $x$, which is in $\dom(\Gamma)$ by generation, and $\Gamma \vdash x : \tPi{y}{A}{B}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:consistency}]
Suppose that $\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$.
By strong normalization, $t$ reduces to a normal term $n$, and by subject reduction, $\cdot \vdash n : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$.
We show that no such $n$ exists, using Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-shape} twice.

\emph{The normal form is a $\lambda$.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-shape}, $n$ is a universe, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or a neutral term.
\begin{itemize}
  \item It is not neutral, because its head would be a variable in the empty context.
  \item It is not a universe or a $\Pi$, because generation would make $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$ convertible to a universe, which confluence rules out.
\end{itemize}
So $n = \tLam{x}{A}{s}$.
By generation, $x : A \vdash s : B$ and $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P} \conv \tPi{x}{A}{B}$ for some $B$.
By confluence, $A \conv \Sort{0}$ and $\subst{P}{P}{z} \conv \subst{B}{x}{z}$ for a fresh $z$, that is, $z \conv \subst{B}{x}{z}$.
Substituting $x$ for $z$ on both sides, which preserves convertibility by (c), gives $x \conv B$.
The body $s$ is normal, because it is a subterm of $n$.
In short, $x : A \vdash s : B$ with $A \conv \Sort{0}$ and $B \conv x$.

\emph{The body cannot exist.}
Let $\Gamma = x : A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-shape}, $s$ is a universe, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or a neutral term.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $s$ is a universe or a $\Pi$, generation makes $B$ convertible to a universe; if $s$ is a $\lambda$, it makes $B$ convertible to a $\Pi$.
    But $B \conv x$, and by confluence a variable is convertible to neither.
  \item If $s$ is neutral, its head is a variable in $\dom(\Gamma) = \{x\}$, so $s = x\;a_1 \cdots a_k$.
    If $k = 0$, then $s = x$, and generation gives $B \conv A$. Then $x \conv B \conv A \conv \Sort{0}$, but a variable is not convertible to a universe.
    If $k \ge 1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-shape} gives $\Gamma \vdash x : C$ with $C$ convertible to a $\Pi$, and generation gives $C \conv A \conv \Sort{0}$.
    Then a $\Pi$ is convertible to a universe, which confluence rules out.
\end{itemize}
Every case leads to a contradiction, so no closed term has type $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$.
\end{proof}

\noindent In words: the only variable available is $x$, whose type is $\Sort{0}$.
It can neither be returned, since $\Sort{0}$ is not $x$, nor be applied to anything, since $\Sort{0}$ is not a function type.
Every other normal term has a universe or a $\Pi$ as its type.
The argument relies on strong normalization to reduce the question to normal terms; that step is where all the difficulty lies.
